concepts.label: A nonzero bounded linear operator is not bounded on the domain

content.statement: Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed vector spaces. A function $f:X\to Y$ is said to be bounded on $X$ if there exists $M>0$ such that $\|f(x)\|\leq M$ for all $x\in X$. Show that a nonzero bounded linear operator $T:X\to Y$ is not bounded on $X$.
content.intuition: Linearity lets one scale a single nonzero output without bound. Bounded linear operator means controlled growth relative to input norm, not bounded image on all of $X$.

assumptions: $X$ and $Y$ are normed vector spaces over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.
$T:X\to Y$ is a nonzero bounded linear operator.

steps.content: Since $T\neq0$, there exists $x_0\in X$ such that $Tx_0\neq0$.
For every scalar $\lambda\in\mathbb K$, linearity gives $T(\lambda x_0)=\lambda Tx_0$.
Taking norms gives $$\|T(\lambda x_0)\|=\|\lambda Tx_0\|=|\lambda|\,\|Tx_0\|.$$ Since $\|Tx_0\|>0$ and $|\lambda|$ can be arbitrarily large, the set $\{\|Tx\|:x\in X\}$ is unbounded.
Therefore there is no $M>0$ such that $\|Tx\|\leq M$ for all $x\in X$. Hence $T$ is not bounded as a function on its whole domain.

content.definition: Approximate difficult objects by simpler ones and pass to a limit.
content.intuition: Prove first for finite/simple pieces, then complete.

content.statement: Every indexed family of nonempty sets admits a choice function.
content.definition: Let $I$ be a set and let $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family of sets such that $A_i\neq\varnothing$ for every $i\in I$. The Axiom of Choice asserts that there exists a function $f:I\to\bigcup_{i\in I}A_i$ such that $f(i)\in A_i$ for every $i\in I$.
content.formal: $$\left[(\forall i\in I)\,A_i\neq\varnothing\right]\Longrightarrow\left[(\exists f:I\to\bigcup_{i\in I}A_i)(\forall i\in I)\,f(i)\in A_i\right].$$
content.intuition: One may select one element from every set in an arbitrary family, even when no explicit or canonical selection rule is available.
content.gloss: Every family of nonempty sets has a simultaneous selection.

concepts.label: Bounded function on a domain

content.statement: A function is bounded on its domain if its entire image lies inside one ball of the codomain.
content.definition: A function $f:X\to Y$ is bounded on $X$ if all values of $f$ have norm bounded above by a single constant.
content.formal: Let $X$ be a set and let $(Y,\|\cdot\|_Y)$ be a normed vector space. A function $f:X\to Y$ is bounded on $X$ iff $\exists M>0\,\forall x\in X:\ \|f(x)\|_Y\le M$.
content.intuition: The whole image $f(X)$ fits inside one ball centered at $0$ in $Y$.
notation: $$\begin{aligned}f:X\to Y\text{ bounded on }X&\iff \exists M>0\\ \forall x\in X:\ \|f(x)\|_Y\le M,\\ f(X)&\subseteq B_Y(0,M).\end{aligned}$$

assumptions: $X$ is a set.
$(Y,\|\cdot\|_Y)$ is a normed vector space.
$f:X\to Y$ is a function.

content.statement: $A\times B$ is the set of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate lies in $A$ and whose second coordinate lies in $B$.
content.definition: The Cartesian product of sets $A$ and $B$ is $$A\times B:=\{(a,b):a\in A,\ b\in B\}.$$
content.formal: $$A\times B:=\{(a,b):a\in A,\ b\in B\}.$$
content.intuition: A product is the ambient set where binary relations and functions live. Choosing the first coordinate from $A$ and the second from $B$ makes $A\times B$ a coordinate system for assignments from $A$ to $B$.

concepts.label: Closed sets are sequentially closed

content.statement: Show that a subset of a metric space $M$ is closed if and only if it is sequentially closed. That is, show that $E$ is a closed subset of $M$ if and only if every convergent sequence in $E$ has its limit in $E$.
content.intuition: Closedness can be tested by sequences in metric spaces: if a sequence stays in the set and converges, its limit cannot escape the set.

assumptions: $M$ is a metric space.
$E$ is a subset of $M$.

steps.content: Let $M$ be a metric space, and let $E$ be a subset of $M$.

First, we will show that if $E$ is closed, then it is sequentially closed. Suppose $E$ is closed, and let $(x_n)$ be a sequence in $E$ that converges to some limit $x \in M$. Since $E$ is closed, it contains all of its limit points, so $x \in E$.

Next, we will show that if $E$ is sequentially closed, then it is closed. Suppose $E$ is sequentially closed, and let $x$ be a limit point of $E$. This means that every neighborhood of $x$ contains a point of $E$ different from $x$. We can construct a sequence $(x_n)$ in $E$ that converges to $x$ by choosing $x_n$ to be a point in $E$ that is within $1/n$ of $x$ for each $n \in \mathbb{N}$. Since $E$ is sequentially closed, the limit of this sequence must be in $E$, so $x \in E$.

We have shown that if $E$ is closed, then it is sequentially closed, and if $E$ is sequentially closed, then it is closed. Therefore, a subset of a metric space $M$ is closed if and only if it is sequentially closed.

content.definition: Preimages of open sets are open; for linear maps between normed spaces this is equivalent to boundedness.
content.intuition: Small input changes produce small output changes.

content.statement: Convergence means that a sequence eventually remains inside every neighborhood of a proposed limit.
content.definition: In a metric or normed space, a sequence converges to a limit if the distance from the terms to that limit tends to zero.
content.formal: $$x_n\to x\iff \forall \varepsilon>0\,\exists N\in\mathbb{N}\,\forall n\ge N:\ d(x_n,x)<\varepsilon.$$
content.intuition: Convergence compares each far-out term to one external object, the limit. This is different from Cauchy, which compares far-out terms to each other.

content.definition: Prove on a dense subset, then extend by continuity.
content.intuition: Control the whole space from a dense core.

content.definition: A method selecting subsequences or objects along a diagonal to satisfy countably many conditions.
content.intuition: Build one object that survives infinitely many requirements.

content.statement: A function $f:A\to B$ comes with a domain $A$ and codomain $B$.
content.definition: The domain is the set of allowed inputs. The codomain is the declared target set in which outputs live.
content.formal: $$f:A\to B,\qquad \operatorname{dom}(f)=A,\qquad \operatorname{codom}(f)=B.$$
content.intuition: The same graph can carry different codomain declarations, so the arrow $A\to B$ is part of the mathematical data, not only decoration.

concepts.label: Function / map

content.statement: A function is a rule assigning to each element of a domain exactly one element of a codomain.
content.definition: A function, also called a map or mapping, from $A$ to $B$ is a subset $f\subseteq A\times B$ such that every $a\in A$ occurs as the first coordinate of exactly one ordered pair in $f$. We write $f(a)$ for that unique second coordinate.
content.formal: $$f:A\to B\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f\subseteq A\times B\ \text{ and }\ \forall a\in A\,\exists! b\in B:\ (a,b)\in f.$$
content.intuition: The bare mathematical arrow is still a set of ordered pairs under the hood. The function condition says each input is used once, so the notation $f(a)$ names one unambiguous output.

assumptions: $A$ is a set.
$B$ is a set.
Each $a\in A$ has exactly one assigned value $f(a)\in B$.

source.citation: standard mathematical terminology; compatible with the existing functional_analysis graph

content.definition: Study of normed, topological, and infinite-dimensional linear spaces and their continuous linear maps.
content.intuition: Linear algebra with topology, completeness, duality, and limits turned on.

concepts.label: If $T$ vanishes on a vector, then $S$ must also vanish on that vector

content.statement: Let $X$ be a normed vector space and let $T,S\in X^*$. Suppose that $T(x)=0$ implies $S(x)=0$ for every $x\in X$. Show that there is a scalar $c$ with $S=cT$, that is, $S(x)=cT(x)$ for all $x\in X$.
content.formal: Let $X$ be a normed vector space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and let $T,S\in X^*$. Then $$\Big(\forall x\in X:\ T(x)=0\implies S(x)=0\Big)\quad\implies\quad\Big(\exists c\in\mathbb K\ \forall x\in X:\ S(x)=cT(x)\Big).$$ Equivalently, $\ker T\subseteq\ker S$ implies $S\in\operatorname{span}\{T\}$. Note the quantifier order: the scalar $c$ is chosen once and must then work for every $x$, so it may not depend on $x$.
content.intuition: The hypothesis says exactly that $\ker T\subseteq\ker S$. A functional is determined by its kernel up to a scalar, because $\ker T$ has codimension at most one: modulo $\ker T$ the space is at most one-dimensional, and a linear map on a one-dimensional space is multiplication by a constant. So $S$ can only be a rescaling of $T$.
content.gloss: The construction of $c$ needs a single vector $x_0$ outside $\ker T$, which exists precisely when $T\neq0$; the degenerate case $T=0$ must be handled separately.

examples.content: If $S=cT$ then $T(x)=0$ gives $S(x)=c\cdot0=0$, so $\ker T\subseteq\ker S$. Hence the two conditions are equivalent: $$\ker T\subseteq\ker S\iff\exists c\in\mathbb K:\ S=cT.$$
examples.label: The converse direction is immediate

examples.content: For $T\neq0$ the decomposition $x=u+\frac{T(x)}{T(x_0)}x_0$ with $u\in\ker T$ exhibits $X=\ker T\oplus\operatorname{span}\{x_0\}$. This is the structural fact the argument turns on, and it is what fails for maps into higher-dimensional targets: the analogous statement for operators $T,S:X\to Y$ with $\dim Y\geq2$ is false.
examples.label: Why $\ker T$ has codimension at most one

assumptions: $X$ is a normed vector space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.
$T,S\in X^*$ are continuous linear functionals.
The hypothesis is the kernel inclusion $\ker T\subseteq\ker S$, quantified over all $x\in X$.
Continuity is not used; the statement holds for arbitrary linear functionals on a vector space.

steps.content: Let $T,S\in X^*$ satisfy $\ker T\subseteq\ker S$. The goal is a single scalar $c\in\mathbb K$, independent of $x$, with $S(x)=cT(x)$ for all $x\in X$.

Suppose first $T=0$. Then $\ker T=X$, so the hypothesis gives $S(x)=0$ for every $x\in X$, i.e. $S=0$. Any $c\in\mathbb K$ then satisfies $S=cT$, for instance $c=0$. This case must be treated separately because the next step requires a vector on which $T$ does not vanish.

Now suppose $T
eq0$. By definition there exists $x_0\in X$ with $T(x_0)
eq0$. Define $$c= rac{S(x_0)}{T(x_0)}\in\mathbb K,$$ which is well defined since $T(x_0)
eq0$. The scalar $c$ is fixed once and for all here, before any $x$ is considered.
Let $x\in X$ be arbitrary and set $$u=x-\frac{T(x)}{T(x_0)}x_0.$$ Applying $T$ and using linearity, $$T(u)=T(x)-\frac{T(x)}{T(x_0)}T(x_0)=T(x)-T(x)=0,$$ so $u\in\ker T$.
Since $\ker T\subseteq\ker S$, we get $S(u)=0$. Expanding by linearity of $S$, $$0=S(u)=S(x)-\frac{T(x)}{T(x_0)}S(x_0).$$
Rearranging and using the definition of $c$, $$S(x)=\frac{T(x)}{T(x_0)}S(x_0)=\frac{S(x_0)}{T(x_0)}T(x)=cT(x).$$ Since $x\in X$ was arbitrary and $c$ was fixed beforehand, $S=cT$ as required.

concepts.label: If a sequence converges in a normed space, then it is bounded. Converse false.

content.statement: Let $X$ be a normed space. A sequence $(x_n)_{\infty n=1}$ in $X$ is said to be bounded if there exists a $M > 0$ such that $\|x_n\| \leq M$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. Show that in a normed space a convergent sequence is bounded. Is the converse true? That is, must a bounded sequence necessarily converge?
content.formal: $$(X,\|\cdot\|)\text{ normed space},\ x_n\to x \implies (x_n) \text{ is bounded}.$$
content.intuition: Convergence means the terms get arbitrarily close to the limit, so they must stay within some fixed distance of the limit.

assumptions: $(X,\|\cdot\|)$ is a normed space.
$$\lim_{n\to\infty} x_n = x \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad \forall \varepsilon > 0,\ \exists N:\ n\ge N \implies \|x_n-x\|<\varepsilon$$.

steps.content: Let $(X,\|\cdot\|)$ be a normed space and suppose $x_n\to x$ in norm. The goal is a single $M\in[0,\infty)$ with $\|x_n\|\leq M$ for every $n\in\mathbb N$, so $M$ may not depend on $n$.

By definition of $x_n\to x$, $$\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists N\in\mathbb N\ \forall k\geq N:\quad\|x_k-x\|<\varepsilon.$$ Apply this with the specific choice $\varepsilon=1$, which is legitimate since $1>0$, to obtain $N\in\mathbb N$ such that $\|x_k-x\|<1$ for all $k\geq N$.
For any $n\geq N$, $$\begin{aligned}\|x_n\|&=\|x_n-x+x\| && \text{add and subtract }x\\ &\leq\|x_n-x\|+\|x\| && \text{triangle inequality}\\ &<1+\|x\| && \text{previous step, }n\geq N.\end{aligned}$$

The indices $n<N$ are finitely many, so $\max_{1\leq n<N}\|x_n\|$ exists as a maximum over a finite set of reals (this is where finiteness is essential; an infinite set of norms need not attain a maximum).

Put $$M=\max\Big\{1+\|x\|,\ \max_{1\leq n<N}\|x_n\|\Big\}.$$ Then $\|x_n\|\leq M$ for every $n\in\mathbb N$: for $n\geq N$ by the calculation, and for $n<N$ by construction of the second term. Hence $(x_n)$ is bounded.

concepts.label: In a metric space, a convergent sequence is Cauchy.

content.statement: Show that in a metric space a convergent sequence is a Cauchy sequence.
content.formal: $$(X,d)\text{ metric space},\ x_n\to x \implies x_n \text{ is Cauchy}.$$
content.intuition: Convergence means the terms get arbitrarily close to the limit, so they must get arbitrarily close to each other.

assumptions: $(X,d)$ is a metric space.
$$\lim_{n\to\infty} x_n = x \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad \forall \varepsilon > 0,\ \exists N:\ n\ge N \implies d(x_n,x)<\varepsilon$$.

steps.content: Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space, and suppose $x_n \to x$. Let $\epsilon > 0$ be arbitrary.
Since $x_n \to x$, for every $\delta > 0$ there exists N in N such that for all k >= N, d(x_k, x) < delta. Choose $\delta = \epsilon/2$. Since $\epsilon > 0$, $\epsilon/2 > 0$.
There exists $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that for all $k >= N, d(x_k, x) < \epsilon/2$.
Let $n,m >= N$. Since the bound holds for every $k >= N$, we get $d(x_n, x) < \epsilon/2$ and $d(x_m, x) < \epsilon/2$.
Using the triangle inequality and symmetry, $d(x_n, x_m) \leq d(x_n, x) + d(x, x_m) = d(x_n, x) + d(x_m, x) < \epsilon/2 + \epsilon/2 = \epsilon$.
Therefore, for every $\epsilon > 0$, there exists $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that for all $n,m >= N$, $d(x_n, x_m) < \epsilon$. Hence $(x_n)$ is Cauchy.

content.statement: The natural numbers are the standard index set for sequences.
content.definition: The set $\mathbb{N}$ is used to enumerate ordered infinite lists, usually starting at either $0$ or $1$ depending on convention.
content.formal: $$\mathbb{N}=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}\quad\text{or}\quad\mathbb{N}=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}.$$
content.intuition: For sequences, $n\in\mathbb{N}$ is the slot number and $x_n$ is the object placed in that slot.

content.statement: An ordered pair $(a,b)$ records two objects in order; $(a,b)=(c,d)$ exactly when $a=c$ and $b=d$.
content.definition: An ordered pair is an object with a first coordinate and a second coordinate. It may be encoded in pure set theory by Kuratowski's definition $(a,b):=\{\{a\},\{a,b\}\}$, but in ordinary use it can be treated as a primitive ordered object.
content.formal: $$(a,b)=(c,d)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a=c\ \text{ and }\ b=d.$$
content.intuition: Sets forget order, but ordered pairs remember it: $\{3,7\}=\{7,3\}$ while $(3,7)\neq(7,3)$. That memory is what makes coordinates, products, relations, and functions possible.

examples.label: A set has no first coordinate; an ordered pair does.

content.statement: A relation from $A$ to $B$ is any subset of the Cartesian product $A\times B$.
content.definition: A relation records which ordered pairs are declared related; a function is a relation with existence and uniqueness of outputs.
content.formal: $$R\subseteq A\times B.$$
content.intuition: A relation is arbitrary wiring between inputs and outputs. A function is the special wiring where every input has exactly one outgoing wire.

concepts.label: Reverse triangle inequality

content.statement: Let $X$ be a normed space. Show that $|\|x\| - \|y\|| \leq \|x - y\|$ for all $x$ and $y$ in $X$. (This is sometimes called the reverse triangle inequality.)
content.formal: $$(X,\|\cdot\|)\text{ normed space},\ |\|x\| - \|y\|| \leq \|x - y\| \quad \forall x,y \in X.$$
content.intuition: The triangle inequality says $\|x+y\| \leq \|x\| + \|y\|$. The reverse triangle inequality says $\|x-y\| \geq |\|x\| - \|y\||$.

assumptions: $(X,\|\cdot\|)$ is a normed space.

steps.content: Let $(X,\|\cdot\|)$ be a normed space, and let $x,y \in X$ be arbitrary.
Using the triangle inequality, we have $\|x\| = \|y + (x - y)\| \leq \|y\| + \|x - y\|$. Rearranging gives $\|x\| - \|y\| \leq \|x - y\|$.
Similarly, we have $\|y\| = \|x + (y - x)\| \leq \|x\| + \|y - x\| = \|x\| + \|x - y\|$. Rearranging gives $\|y\| - \|x\| \leq \|x - y\|$.
Combining the two inequalities, we get $-\|x - y\| \leq \|x\| - \|y\| \leq \|x - y\|$. Therefore, $|\|x\| - \|y\|| \leq \|x - y\|$.

content.statement: The scalar field is either the real numbers or the complex numbers.
content.intuition: Functional analysis is usually developed over the reals or complexes, and some results depend on this choice.

concepts.label: Scalar limit to infinity

content.statement: For real scalars, $\lambda\to+\infty$ and $\lambda\to-\infty$ are meaningful; for complex scalars, escape to infinity is written $|\lambda|\to\infty$.
content.definition: The real field has an order, so one-sided limits to $+\infty$ and $-\infty$ are meaningful. The complex field has no natural order, so unbounded escape is expressed using the modulus condition $|\lambda|\to\infty$.
content.formal: $$\mathbb K=\mathbb R:\ \lambda\to+\infty\text{ or }\lambda\to-\infty,\qquad \mathbb K=\mathbb C:\ |\lambda|\to\infty.$$
content.intuition: Real scalars escape to the right or left on a line. Complex scalars escape every disk centered at zero; there is no distinguished positive direction.

assumptions: $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.
$|\cdot|$ denotes the usual absolute value on $\mathbb R$ or modulus on $\mathbb C$.

content.statement: The term function is more general/weaker than operator; operator is more specific/stronger in functional-analysis usage.
content.definition: A semantic relation saying that 'function/map' imposes fewer assumptions, while 'operator' adds contextual structure such as vector-space, normed-space, or linear structure.
content.formal: $\{\text{operators}\}\subseteq \{\text{functions/maps}\}$ as terminology classes, while every operator is still a function as set-theoretic data.
content.intuition: Function is the raw arrow. Operator is the arrow with structure attached. Same underlying species, different amount of mathematical baggage.

source.citation: derived semantic clarification from standard functional-analysis convention

concepts.label: Sequence

content.statement: A sequence in a set $S$ is a function $\varphi:\mathbb{N}\to S$, usually written $(f_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ when $f_n=\varphi(n)$.
content.definition: A sequence in $S$ is a function from the natural numbers to $S$. As set-theoretic data it is the graph $$\{(n,f_n):n\in\mathbb{N}\}\subseteq\mathbb{N}\times S.$$
content.formal: $$\varphi:\mathbb{N}\to S,\qquad f_n:=\varphi(n),\qquad (f_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}=\{(n,f_n):n\in\mathbb{N}\}.$$
content.intuition: The terms $f_1,f_2,\ldots$ live inside the sequence; a limit $f$, when it exists, is a separate object the sequence approaches. Reusing the same letter for the sequence and its limit hides this distinction.
notation: $\varphi:\mathbb{N}\to S \text{ is a sequence in } S$

examples.content: The alternating sequence $0,1,0,1,\ldots$ in $S=\{0,1\}$, truncated to its first three terms, is $$\{(1,0),(2,1),(3,0)\}.$$
examples.label: Alternating sequence $(0,1,0,1,\ldots)$ in $S=\{0,1\}$

examples.content: The constant sequence $f_n=g$ for all $n$ is $$\{(n,g):n\in\mathbb{N}\}=\{(1,g),(2,g),(3,g),\ldots\}.$$ The second coordinate repeats, but the ordered pairs are distinct because their first coordinates differ.
examples.label: Constant sequence $g,g,g,\ldots$ in $S$

examples.content: From the perspective of Set Theory, a sequence is just a set of ordered pairs. The sequence $f_n=g$ for all $n$ is the set of ordered pairs $$\begin{aligned} &\{(1,g),(2,g),(3,g),\ldots\}\\ &=\{(n,g):n\in\mathbb{N}\}\\ &=\{\{\{n\},\{n,g\}\}:n\in\mathbb{N}\}\\ &\subseteq \mathbb{N}\times S.\end{aligned}$$
examples.label: Sequences viewed from Set Theory

assumptions: $S$ is a set.
The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ are the standard set of counting numbers.
A sequence is a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $S$, so it is a set of ordered pairs with first coordinates in $\mathbb{N}$ and second coordinates in $S$.

concepts.label: Sequence limit versus variable limit

content.statement: A sequence limit varies over natural-number indices; a variable limit varies over a larger domain such as $[0,\infty)$, $\mathbb R$, or $\mathbb C$.
content.definition: The expression $\lim_{n\to\infty}a_n$ is a limit of a sequence $a:\mathbb N\to S$. The expression $\lim_{t\to\infty}f(t)$ is a limit of a function whose variable moves through a domain with a meaningful notion of escaping to infinity.
content.formal: $$a:\mathbb N\to S,\qquad a_n=a(n),\qquad \lim_{n\to\infty}a_n\text{ is a sequence limit}.$$
content.intuition: A sequence limit samples the path at integer indices. A variable limit may use every allowed point in the domain. In proofs, the sequence version is often enough.

assumptions: $(a_n)$ is a sequence.
$f$ is a function whose domain has a meaningful notion of tending to infinity.

content.statement: A set is an unordered collection of objects, determined entirely by its members.
content.definition: A set is treated extensionally: two sets are equal exactly when they have the same elements. Order and repetition do not create new sets.
content.formal: $$A=B\iff \forall x\,(x\in A\leftrightarrow x\in B).$$
content.intuition: The set is the floor of the construction. Once membership is fixed, the object is fixed; listing order and repeated listings are invisible.

concepts.label: The derivative at zero defines an unbounded linear functional on $C^{(1)}[0,1]$

content.statement: Let $C^{(1)}[0,1]$ be the space of continuously differentiable functions on $[0,1]$, equipped with $\|f\|=\max_{t\in[0,1]}|f(t)|$. Show that $B(f)=f'(0)$ defines a linear functional that is not bounded.
content.intuition: The supremum norm controls function height, but not derivative steepness. Functions can stay uniformly bounded while their derivative at one point becomes arbitrarily large.

assumptions: $C^{(1)}[0,1]$ is equipped with the norm $\|f\|=\max_{t\in[0,1]}|f(t)|$.
$B:C^{(1)}[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ is defined by $B(f)=f'(0)$.

steps.content: For $f,g\in C^{(1)}[0,1]$ and $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, $$B(\alpha f+g)=(\alpha f+g)'(0)=\alpha f'(0)+g'(0)=\alpha B(f)+B(g).$$ Hence $B$ is linear.
For each $n\in\mathbb N$, define $f_n(t)=\sin(nt)$. Then $f_n\in C^{(1)}[0,1]$ and $\|f_n\|\leq1$.
Since $f_n'(t)=n\cos(nt)$, we have $$B(f_n)=f_n'(0)=n.$$
If $B$ were bounded, there would be $C>0$ such that $|B(f)|\leq C\|f\|$ for all $f$. Applying this to $f_n$ gives $n=|B(f_n)|\leq C\|f_n\|\leq C$, impossible for all $n$.
Thus $B$ is linear but not bounded.

concepts.label: The integral defines a bounded linear functional on $C[0, 1]$

content.statement: Let $C[0, 1]$ be the space of continuous functions on $[0, 1]$ and define a norm $\|\cdot\|$ on $C[0, 1]$ by $\|f\| = \max_{t \in [0,1]} |f(t)|$. Show that the map $A(f) = \int_0^1 f(x) dx$ defines a bounded linear functional on the normed vector space $(C[0, 1], \|\cdot\|)$.
content.formal: $$C[0, 1]\text{ space of continuous functions},\ \|f\| = \max_{t \in [0,1]} |f(t)|,\ A(f) = \int_0^1 f(x) dx \implies A \text{ is a bounded linear functional on }(C[0, 1], \|\cdot\|).$$
content.intuition: The integral is linear and can be bounded by the maximum value of the function, so it defines a bounded linear functional on the space of continuous functions with the supremum norm.

assumptions: $C[0, 1]$ is the space of continuous functions on $[0, 1]$.

steps.content: Let $C[0, 1]$ be the space of continuous functions on $[0, 1]$ equipped with the norm $\|f\| = \max_{t \in [0,1]} |f(t)|$. Define the map $A : C[0, 1] \to \mathbb{R}$ by $A(f) = \int_0^1 f(x) dx$.

To show that $A$ is linear, let $f, g \in C[0, 1]$ and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. We have: $$A(\alpha f + g) = \int_0^1 (\alpha f(x) + g(x)) dx = \alpha \int_0^1 f(x) dx + \int_0^1 g(x) dx = \alpha A(f) + A(g).$$ Thus, $A$ is linear.

To show that $A$ is bounded, we need to find a constant $M > 0$ such that $|A(f)| \leq M \|f\|$ for all $f \in C[0, 1]$. Since $\|f\| = \max_{t \in [0,1]} |f(t)|$, we have: $$|A(f)| = \left|\int_0^1 f(x) dx\right| \leq \int_0^1 |f(x)| dx \leq \int_0^1 \|f\| dx = \|f\|.$$ Thus, we can take $M = 1$, and we have $|A(f)| \leq M \|f\|$ for all $f \in C[0, 1]$. Therefore, $A$ is a bounded linear functional on $(C[0, 1], \|\cdot\|)$.
We have shown that $A$ is linear and bounded, so $A$ defines a bounded linear functional on the normed vector space $(C[0, 1], \|\cdot\|)$.

concepts.label: Triangle Inequality

content.statement: In a normed space, the norm of a sum is at most the sum of the norms.
content.definition: The triangle inequality is one of the defining axioms of a norm.
content.formal: Let $(X,\|\cdot\|)$ be a normed space. Then for all $x,y\in X$, $$\|x+y\|\leq\|x\|+\|y\|.$$
content.intuition: The direct path from $0$ to $x+y$ is no longer than going first to $x$ and then from $x$ to $x+y$.

assumptions: $(X,\|\cdot\|)$ is a normed space.

concepts.label: Tychonoff's Theorem

content.statement: An arbitrary product of compact topological spaces is compact in the product topology.
content.formal: Let $I$ be any index set and $(K_i,\mathcal T_i)_{i\in I}$ a family of compact topological spaces. Then $$P=\prod_{i\in I}K_i$$ is compact in the product topology, i.e. the initial topology induced by the projections $\pi_j:P\to K_j$. The index set $I$ may be uncountable; this is the case that matters in applications, where $I=X$ is the whole normed space.
content.intuition: Compactness survives arbitrary products, which is surprising because the product topology is very coarse: a basic open set constrains only finitely many coordinates. That coarseness is exactly what makes the theorem true, and it is why weak-star compactness of the dual ball comes for free once the ball is realised inside a product of discs.
content.gloss: The strength is in the arbitrary index set. Finite and countable products are much easier; the general case is equivalent to the axiom of choice.

examples.content: Tychonoff for arbitrary compact spaces is equivalent to the axiom of choice (Kelley). For compact Hausdorff spaces it is strictly weaker, being equivalent to the ultrafilter lemma. Since discs in $\mathbb K$ are compact Hausdorff, Banach-Alaoglu needs only the ultrafilter lemma, not full choice.
examples.label: Equivalence with choice

examples.content: The result is specific to the product topology. The box topology on an infinite product of compact spaces is strictly finer and destroys compactness: $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}$ with the box topology is discrete, hence non-compact, while with the product topology it is the compact Cantor set.
examples.label: Failure for other topologies

assumptions: Each factor $K_i$ is compact.
$P$ carries the product topology, not the box topology.
Some choice principle is assumed: full AC in general, the ultrafilter lemma in the compact Hausdorff case.

concepts.label: $\ell^p$ norms on $\mathbb{R}^2$

content.statement: The same vector space $\mathbb{R}^2$ carries different norm geometries: diamond, round, square, and smooth intermediate unit balls.
content.definition: For $1\leq p<\infty$, the $\ell^p$ norm on $\mathbb{R}^2$ is $\|(x_1,x_2)\|_p=(|x_1|^p+|x_2|^p)^{1/p}$, while $\|(x_1,x_2)\|_\infty=\max(|x_1|,|x_2|)$.
content.intuition: Changing the norm changes what one unit of reach looks like: $\ell^1$ gives a diamond, $\ell^2$ a circle, $\ell^\infty$ a square, and $\ell^p$ interpolates between these shapes.

assumptions: The underlying vector space is $\mathbb{R}^2$.
$1\leq p<\infty$ for the smooth $\ell^p$ family.

content.definition: Sequence spaces of $p$-summable scalar sequences, equipped with the $p$-norm.
content.formal: $$\begin{aligned}\ell^p&=\left\{x=(x_n):\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}|x_n|^p<\infty\right\},\quad 1\leq p<\infty,\\ \|x\|_p&=\left(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}|x_n|^p\right)^{1/p},\\ \ell^\infty&=\{x=(x_n):\sup_n |x_n|<\infty\},\quad \|x\|_\infty=\sup_n |x_n|.\end{aligned}$$
content.intuition: The $\ell^p$ spaces are discrete model Banach spaces. Their standard basis vectors all have norm one, but in infinite dimensions those points do not cluster in norm.

examples.content: For the standard basis vector $e_n=(0,\ldots,0,1,0,\ldots)$, $\|e_n\|_p=1$ for every $n$ and every $1\leq p\leq\infty$.
examples.label: Basis vectors witness the noncompactness of infinite-dimensional unit balls.

content.definition: A Banach space is a normed vector space in which every norm-Cauchy sequence converges in norm to a point of the same space.
content.formal: A normed vector space $(X,\|\cdot\|)$ is Banach if it is complete as a metric space under the metric $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$.
content.formula: $$\begin{aligned} (X,\|\cdot\|)\text{ is Banach} &\iff (X,d)\text{ is complete, where }d(x,y)=\|x-y\| \\ &\iff \forall (x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\in X^{\mathbb N},\ \left[\forall \varepsilon>0\ \exists N\in\mathbb N\ \forall m,n\ge N:\ \|x_n-x_m\|<\varepsilon\right] \\ &\qquad\Rightarrow \exists x\in X\ \forall \varepsilon>0\ \exists N\in\mathbb N\ \forall n\ge N:\ \|x_n-x\|<\varepsilon. \end{aligned}$$
content.intuition: A Banach space is a normed space with no missing Cauchy limits. If a sequence becomes arbitrarily close to itself in the norm, then it actually converges to a point already inside the space.
notation: $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\in X^{\mathbb N}$ means a sequence in $X$

content.definition: Continuous scalar-valued functions on a compact Hausdorff space K with supremum norm.
content.formal: C(K) with ||f||_infty=sup_{x in K}|f(x)|.
content.intuition: Continuous functions as a Banach space.

concepts.label: Cauchy sequence

content.statement: A sequence in a metric space is Cauchy if, eventually, all of its terms are arbitrarily close to each other.
content.definition: A Cauchy sequence is a sequence whose tails have arbitrarily small diameter.
content.formal: Let $(M,d)$ be a metric space and let $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence in $M$. The sequence $(x_n)$ is Cauchy if and only if $$\forall \varepsilon>0\,\exists N\in\mathbb{N}\,\forall m,n\ge N:\ d(x_m,x_n)<\varepsilon.$$
content.formula: $$\begin{aligned} (x_n)\text{ is Cauchy} &\iff \forall \varepsilon>0\,\exists N\in\mathbb{N}\,\forall m,n\ge N:\ d(x_m,x_n)<\varepsilon \\ &\iff \operatorname{diam}\{x_n:n\ge N\}\to 0\text{ as }N\to\infty \\ &\iff d(x_m,x_n)\to 0\text{ as }m,n\to\infty. \end{aligned}$$
content.intuition: A Cauchy sequence becomes internally stable: sufficiently far out, its terms are close to each other, independently of whether they converge to a point of the space.

assumptions: $(M,d)$ is a metric space.
$(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is a sequence with $x_n\in M$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$.

concepts.label: Closed subspace

content.statement: A closed subspace is a linear subspace that is closed in the ambient topology.
content.definition: A linear subspace containing all limits of convergent sequences from itself, in the ambient norm/topology.
content.formal: $$M\le X,\quad M=\overline{M}.$$
content.intuition: A subspace with no missing limit points, so quotient constructions behave instead of collapsing into nonsense.

assumptions: $X$ is a normed or topological vector space.
$M$ is a linear subspace of $X$.

content.definition: The closed unit ball of a normed space is the set of vectors with norm at most one.
content.intuition: The closed unit ball is the basic test shape for normed-space geometry. Its convexity is the triangle inequality, its symmetry is absolute homogeneity, and its compactness behavior separates finite-dimensional from infinite-dimensional analysis.

content.definition: A topological space or subset is compact if every open cover admits a finite subcover.
content.formal: Let $(Y,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space and $K\subseteq Y$. Then $$K\ \text{compact}\quad:\Longleftrightarrow\quad\forall\,\mathcal U\subseteq\mathcal T\ \text{with}\ K\subseteq\bigcup\mathcal U:\ \exists U_1,\dots,U_n\in\mathcal U\ \text{with}\ K\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^nU_i.$$ Equivalent formulations in a general topological space: every net in $K$ has a subnet converging in $K$; every family of closed subsets of $K$ with the finite intersection property has nonempty intersection. Sequential compactness, $$\forall(y_n)\subseteq K\ \exists\ \text{subsequence}\ (y_{n_k})\ \exists y\in K:\ y_{n_k}\to y,$$ is equivalent to compactness in metric spaces but not in general.
content.intuition: Compactness is topological finiteness. In metric spaces it can be detected by sequences, but in the weak and weak-star topologies, which are typically not metrizable, sequences are too weak an instrument and nets are needed.
content.gloss: The compact-versus-sequentially-compact gap is exactly what makes Banach-Alaoglu insufficient on its own for subsequence extraction, and why separability or Eberlein-Smulian is invoked.

examples.content: In $\mathbb R^n$ or $\mathbb C^n$ a set is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded. This is the fact that makes each scalar disc $\{\lambda:|\lambda|\leq\|x\|\}$ compact in the proof of Banach-Alaoglu.
examples.label: Heine-Borel in $\mathbb K^n$

examples.content: The two notions diverge outside metric spaces. With $X=\ell^\infty$, the ball $B_{X^*}$ is weak-star compact by Banach-Alaoglu yet not weak-star sequentially compact. So compactness of a ball does not by itself license passing to a convergent subsequence.
examples.label: Compact but not sequentially compact

examples.content: If $K$ is compact and $F\subseteq K$ is closed, then $F$ is compact; and in a Hausdorff space compact sets are closed. Both directions are used in the proof of Banach-Alaoglu, the first to cut $\Phi(B_{X^*})$ out of the product.
examples.label: Closed subset of a compact space

content.definition: Use finite subcovers, convergent subsequences, or compactness to extract limiting structure.
content.intuition: Turn infinite behavior into finite or convergent behavior.

content.statement: Completeness means that every Cauchy sequence in the space converges to a limit inside the same space.
content.definition: A metric space is complete if every Cauchy sequence in the space converges to a point of the space.
content.formal: $$X\text{ complete}\iff \forall (x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\in X^{\mathbb N},\ \bigl[(x_n)\text{ is Cauchy}\Rightarrow \exists x\in X:\ x_n\to x\bigr].$$
content.intuition: A Cauchy sequence behaves as if it is approaching a limit, using only distances between its own terms. Completeness says that such a limit is not missing from the space.
notation: $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\in X^{\mathbb N}$ means a sequence in $X$
$\{x_n:n\in\mathbb N\}\subseteq X$ means the range of the sequence lies in $X$

concepts.label: Convex set

content.statement: A subset of a vector space is convex if it contains the line segment joining every pair of its points.
content.definition: Let $X$ be a vector space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and let $C\subseteq X$. The set $C$ is convex if every convex combination of two points of $C$ belongs to $C$.
content.formal: $$C\text{ is convex}\iff(\forall x,y\in C)(\forall\lambda\in[0,1])\;\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y\in C.$$
content.intuition: Every line segment between two points of the set remains entirely inside the set.
content.gloss: A subset containing every line segment between its points.

examples.content: Every vector subspace and every norm ball are convex.
The unit circle $\{x\in\mathbb R^2:\|x\|=1\}$ is not convex.

assumptions: $X$ is a vector space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.
$C\subseteq X$.

concepts.label: Equivalent norms

content.statement: Two norms are equivalent when each controls the other up to fixed positive constants.
content.definition: Norms $\|\cdot\|_a$ and $\|\cdot\|_b$ on the same vector space are equivalent if they bound each other by constant multiples.
content.formal: $$\|\cdot\|_a\sim\|\cdot\|_b\iff \exists c,C>0\ \forall x\in X:\ c\|x\|_a\leq\|x\|_b\leq C\|x\|_a.$$
content.intuition: Equivalent norms may draw different unit balls, but neither geometry can make a vector infinitely smaller or larger than the other. Each unit ball is sandwiched between scaled copies of the other.

assumptions: Both norms are defined on the same vector space $X$.

concepts.label: Finite-dimensional norm equivalence

content.statement: Every two norms on a finite-dimensional vector space are equivalent.
content.formal: If $\dim X<\infty$ and $\|\cdot\|_a,\|\cdot\|_b$ are norms on $X$, then $$\exists c,C>0\ \forall x\in X:\ c\|x\|_a\leq\|x\|_b\leq C\|x\|_a.$$
content.intuition: In finite dimensions, every norm unit ball can be squeezed between two scaled copies of any other. This is why different finite-dimensional norms induce the same open sets and convergence.

assumptions: $X$ is finite-dimensional.

steps.content: Let $X$ be finite-dimensional and let $\|\cdot\|_a$, $\|\cdot\|_b$ be two norms on $X$.
Choose a basis of $X$ and identify $X$ algebraically with $\mathbb K^n$.
The unit sphere $S_a=\{x:\|x\|_a=1\}$ is compact in finite dimensions, and the function $x\mapsto\|x\|_b$ is continuous on $S_a$.
Since $S_a$ is compact and $\|x\|_b>0$ on $S_a$, there exist $m,M>0$ such that $m\leq\|x\|_b\leq M$ for all $x\in S_a$.
For $x\neq0$, apply the sphere estimate to $x/\|x\|_a$ to get $$m\|x\|_a\leq\|x\|_b\leq M\|x\|_a.$$ The case $x=0$ is immediate.

concepts.label: Hoelder's inequality

content.statement: The integral of a product is bounded by the product of the conjugate-exponent norms.
content.formal: Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be conjugate exponents, $\frac1p+\frac1q=1$. Then for all measurable $f,g$, $$\int_\Omega|fg|\,d\mu\leq\|f\|_p\,\|g\|_q,$$ so $f\in L^p$ and $g\in L^q$ imply $fg\in L^1$. For $p=q=2$ this is the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. Equality holds if and only if $|f|^p$ and $|g|^q$ are proportional almost everywhere (for $1<p<\infty$).
content.intuition: The conjugate relation $\frac1p+\frac1q=1$ is exactly the balance making the product integrable: whatever integrability one factor lacks, the other must supply. It is the inequality that makes the pairing $(f,g)\mapsto\int f\overline g$ bounded, hence the reason $L^q$ embeds into $(L^p)^*$.
content.gloss: Everything compared here is a number: both sides are extended reals in $[0,\infty]$.

examples.content: If $\frac1p+\frac1q<1$ the inequality fails in general. On $\Omega=(0,1)$ with Lebesgue measure take $f(t)=g(t)=t^{-1/2}$, which lies in $L^p$ for $p<2$; for $p=q=3/2$ the product $fg(t)=t^{-1}$ is not integrable, while both norms are finite.
examples.label: Conjugacy cannot be relaxed

examples.content: Minkowski's inequality $\|f+g\|_p\leq\|f\|_p+\|g\|_p$ is proved by applying Hoelder to $\int|f+g|^{p-1}|f|$ and $\int|f+g|^{p-1}|g|$, using that $(p-1)q=p$. So Hoelder is what makes $\|\cdot\|_p$ a norm.
examples.label: Gives the triangle inequality for $\|\cdot\|_p$

assumptions: $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ is a measure space; no $\sigma$-finiteness is needed.
$p,q$ are conjugate: $\frac1p+\frac1q=1$, with the conventions $1/\infty=0$.

concepts.label: Incomplete normed spaces as non-examples of Banach spaces

content.definition: Normed spaces with Cauchy sequences that do not converge inside the space.
content.intuition: Shows completeness is not cosmetic in Banach-space theorems.

concepts.label: Infinite-dimensional unit balls need not be compact

content.statement: In infinite-dimensional normed spaces, the closed unit ball is generally not compact in the norm topology.
content.formal: In $\ell^p$ for $1\leq p<\infty$, the standard basis vectors $(e_n)$ satisfy $\|e_n\|_p=1$ and $\|e_n-e_m\|_p=2^{1/p}$ for $n\neq m$. Hence $(e_n)$ has no norm-convergent subsequence.
content.intuition: The unit ball can contain infinitely many points that remain a fixed distance apart. This is the geometric rupture between finite-dimensional norm geometry and Banach-space theory.

assumptions: The norm topology is used.
The space is infinite-dimensional; the displayed model is $\ell^p$.

content.definition: Equivalence classes of p-integrable measurable functions.
content.formal: Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $1\leq p<\infty$. Then $$L^p(\Omega)=\Big\{f:\Omega\to\mathbb K\ \text{measurable}\ :\ \int_\Omega|f|^p\,d\mu<\infty\Big\}\Big/\sim,$$ where $f\sim g$ means $f=g$ $\mu$-almost everywhere, normed by $$\|f\|_p=\Big(\int_\Omega|f|^p\,d\mu\Big)^{1/p}.$$ For $p=\infty$, $\|f\|_\infty=\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{\Omega}|f|$. Quotienting by almost-everywhere equality is what makes $\|\cdot\|_p$ positive definite rather than a seminorm.
content.intuition: Function-space analogue of ell^p.

concepts.label: Limit of a sequence

content.statement: A limit is the object that a sequence eventually gets arbitrarily close to, measured by the ambient metric or norm.
content.definition: In a metric space, $(x_n)$ converges to $x$ if every positive distance tolerance is eventually satisfied. In a normed space, this means $\|x_n-x\|\to0$ because the norm induces the metric $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$.
content.formal: $$x_n\to x\text{ in }(M,d)\iff \forall\varepsilon>0\,\exists N\in\mathbb N\,\forall n\ge N:\ d(x_n,x)<\varepsilon.$$
content.intuition: The sequence is the indexed list; the limit is a separate point. A metric or norm is what makes the phrase 'gets close to' precise.

assumptions: $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ is a sequence in a metric or normed space.
$x$ is an element of the ambient space.
The ambient space has a metric, or has a norm inducing a metric.

content.definition: A topological vector space whose topology has a local base at zero consisting of convex sets.
content.intuition: A TVS with enough convex geometry for separation theorems.

concepts.label: Metric induced by a norm

content.statement: Every norm on a vector space induces a metric by measuring the norm of the difference.
content.definition: The metric induced by a norm is the distance function $d_X(x,y)=\|x-y\|_X$.
content.formal: Let $(X,\|\cdot\|_X)$ be a normed vector space. Define $$d_X(x,y)=\|x-y\|_X.$$ Then $d_X$ is a metric on $X$.
content.intuition: Distance is the norm-cost of the displacement from one vector to the other. Metric balls are just translated and rescaled copies of the norm unit ball.

assumptions: $(X,\|\cdot\|_X)$ is a normed vector space.

content.definition: A set equipped with a distance function satisfying positivity, symmetry, and the triangle inequality.
content.formal: $(M,d)$ with $d:M\times M\to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$, $d(x,y)=0\Leftrightarrow x=y$, $d(x,y)=d(y,x)$, $d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)$.
content.intuition: A space where convergence and Cauchy sequences can be measured.

concepts.label: Minkowski functional

content.statement: A convex, balanced, absorbing set around zero defines a gauge by asking how much the set must be scaled to reach a vector.
content.definition: The Minkowski functional of a set $B\subseteq X$ is $p_B(x)=\inf\{t>0:x\in tB\}$.
content.formal: Let $B\subseteq X$ be convex, balanced, absorbing, and with $p_B(x)=0$ only for $x=0$. Then $$p_B(x)=\inf\{t>0:x\in tB\}$$ is a norm whose unit ball is $B$ up to closure.
content.intuition: Instead of starting with a formula for length, start with the one-unit shape. The norm of $x$ is the scale factor needed to stretch that shape until it contains $x$.

assumptions: $B$ is convex, balanced, absorbing, and contains $0$.
Additional separation from $0$ is needed for the gauge to be a norm rather than only a seminorm.

concepts.label: Norm

content.statement: A norm is a length function on a vector space satisfying positive definiteness, absolute homogeneity, and the triangle inequality.
content.definition: A norm is a function assigning a nonnegative length to each vector in a vector space, compatible with scalar multiplication and vector addition. Its unit ball is convex, balanced, absorbing, and determines the norm.
content.formal: Let $X$ be a vector space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. A norm on $X$ is a function $\|\cdot\|:X\to[0,\infty)$ such that for all $x,y\in X$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb K$, $$\begin{aligned} &\|x\|\ge 0,\\ &\|x\|=0\iff x=0,\\ &\|\lambda x\|=|\lambda|\,\|x\|,\\ &\|x+y\|\le \|x\|+\|y\|. \end{aligned}$$
content.intuition: A norm is the analytic version of length, but the best picture is its unit ball: vectors inside cost at most one unit of size, and every other length is read by scaling that shape until it reaches the vector.

examples.label: The same vector can have different sizes in different norm geometries.

assumptions: $X$ is a vector space.
The scalar field is $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$.

concepts.label: Normed Vector Space

content.statement: A normed vector space is a vector space equipped with a norm, which induces a metric and a compatible topology.
content.definition: A normed vector space is a vector space $X$ over $\mathbb K$ together with a norm $\|\cdot\|_X$ on $X$. The norm induces a metric $d_X(x,y)=\|x-y\|_X$ and a compatible topology $\tau_X$.
content.formal: A normed vector space is an ordered pair $(X,\|\cdot\|_X)$ where $X$ is a vector space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and $\|\cdot\|_X$ is a norm on $X$. The norm induces a metric $d_X(x,y)=\|x-y\|_X$ and a compatible topology $\tau_X$.
content.intuition: A normed vector space is linear algebra with a calibrated notion of size. Its unit ball is the local shape of the geometry, and translating that ball through the space gives distance, convergence, Cauchy sequences, continuity, bounded linear maps, and completeness.

assumptions: $X$ is a vector space.
$\|\cdot\|_X$ is a norm on $X$.

concepts.label: Quotient map

content.statement: The quotient map sends a vector to its coset.
content.definition: The canonical surjective linear map from a space onto its quotient by a subspace.
content.formal: $$Q:X\to X/Y,\qquad Qx=x+Y.$$
content.intuition: Forget the component lying in Y.

assumptions: Y is a closed subspace of X.

concepts.label: Quotient space

content.statement: Let $X$ be a normed vector space and $Y \subseteq X$ a closed linear subspace. The quotient space $X/Y$ is the set of equivalence classes of vectors modulo $Y$, where two vectors are equivalent if their difference lies in $Y$.
content.definition: The quotient construction identifies all vectors differing by an element of $Y$, effectively collapsing $Y$ into the zero element. Each element of $X/Y$ is a coset $x+Y$, representing an affine translate of $Y$. The quotient inherits a natural vector space structure, and when $Y$ is closed, it becomes a normed space under the quotient norm.
content.formal: $$\begin{aligned} x &\sim y \iff x-y \in Y,\\ X/Y &= \{x+Y : x \in X\},\\ \alpha(x+Y) &= \alpha x + Y,\\ (x+Y)+(z+Y) &= (x+z)+Y,\\ \|x+Y\|_{X/Y} &= \inf_{y \in Y} \|x-y\|_X. \end{aligned}$$
content.intuition: A quotient space forgets directions inside the subspace $Y$. Moving along $Y$ does not change your position in $X/Y$, so each coset behaves like a single point. Geometrically, $X/Y$ measures only the directions transverse to $Y$.

assumptions: X is a normed vector space.
Y is a linear subspace of X.
Y is closed if the quotient norm is required to be non-degenerate.
If X is Banach and Y is closed, then X/Y is Banach.
properties: The canonical quotient map $q : X \to X/Y$ given by $q(x)=x+Y$ is linear and surjective.
dim($X/Y$) = dim($X$) - dim($Y$) in the finite-dimensional case.
If $T : X \to Z$ is linear with $Y \subseteq \ker(T)$, then $T$ factors uniquely through $X/Y$.

source.citation: Standard construction; see quotient spaces in linear and functional analysis

concepts.label: Riesz: compact unit ball characterises finite dimension

content.statement: The closed unit ball of a normed space is compact in the norm topology if and only if the space is finite-dimensional.
content.formal: Let $X$ be a normed vector space over $\mathbb K$. Then $$B_X\ \text{is norm compact}\iff\dim X<\infty.$$ The nontrivial direction rests on Riesz's lemma: if $Y\subsetneq X$ is a proper closed subspace and $0<\theta<1$, then $$\exists x_\theta\in X,\ \|x_\theta\|=1:\quad\operatorname{dist}(x_\theta,Y)=\inf_{y\in Y}\|x_\theta-y\|\geq\theta.$$ Iterating with $\theta=1/2$ produces a sequence $(x_n)\subseteq B_X$ with $\|x_n-x_m\|\geq1/2$ for $n\neq m$, which has no convergent subsequence.
content.intuition: In infinite dimensions there is always room to pick a new unit vector staying a fixed distance from the span of all previous ones, so the unit ball contains an infinite $1/2$-separated set. This is the precise reason every compactness theorem in Banach space theory must weaken the topology, and it is the counterexample that gives Banach-Alaoglu its content.
content.gloss: Read as a negative result it says: norm compactness of $B_X$ is not something extra hypotheses can buy in infinite dimensions.

examples.content: For $1\leq p<\infty$ the standard basis satisfies $\|e_n\|_p=1$ and $\|e_n-e_m\|_p=2^{1/p}$ for $n\neq m$, giving the separated sequence directly without invoking Riesz's lemma.
examples.label: Explicit separated sequence in $\ell^p$

examples.content: In $\ell^1=(c_0)^*$ the ball $B_{\ell^1}$ is not norm compact by this result, yet is weak-star compact by Banach-Alaoglu. The same set is compact in one topology and not in the other, which is what makes the choice of topology in Alaoglu load-bearing rather than decorative.
examples.label: Contrast with Banach-Alaoglu

assumptions: $X$ is a normed vector space; completeness is not required.
The topology is the norm topology.
Riesz's lemma needs $Y$ closed and proper; the constant $\theta$ cannot in general be taken equal to $1$.

content.definition: A vector space with a topology making addition and scalar multiplication continuous.
content.intuition: A vector space where limits are compatible with linear operations.

content.definition: The topology generated by open metric balls.
content.intuition: Open sets are built from distance balls.

content.definition: A set with addition and scalar multiplication satisfying the vector space axioms over a field.
content.intuition: The algebraic stage on which linear combinations make sense.

content.definition: The Banach space of scalar sequences converging to zero with the supremum norm.
content.formal: $$c_0=\{x \in \ell^\infty: x_n \to 0\}.$$
content.intuition: A canonical non-reflexive Banach space.

concepts.label: Bounded Linear Functional

content.statement: A bounded linear functional is a bounded linear operator from a normed space to the scalar field.
content.definition: A bounded linear functional on a normed space $X$ is a bounded linear operator $f:X\to \mathbb{K}$, where $\mathbb{K}$ is the scalar field (either $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$).
content.formal: Let $(X,\|\cdot\|_X)$ be a normed vector space over $\mathbb{K}\in\{\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C}\}$. A bounded linear functional on $X$ is a linear map $f:X\to \mathbb{K}$ such that $$\exists C\ge 0\,\forall x\in X:\ |f(x)|\le C\|x\|_X.$$
content.intuition: A bounded linear functional is a way to assign a scalar value to each vector in a way that is linear and does not grow faster than a constant times the norm of the vector.
notation: $$f\in X^\ast=\mathcal{B}(X,\mathbb{K})\iff f\text{ is linear and }\exists C\ge 0\ \forall x\in X:\ |f(x)|\le C\|x\|_X.$$

examples.content: The evaluation functional $\delta_x:X^\ast\to \mathbb{K}$ defined by $\delta_x(f)=f(x)$ is a bounded linear functional on $X^\ast$.
examples.label: Evaluation at a fixed vector is a bounded linear functional on the dual space.

assumptions: $(X,\|\cdot\|_X)$ is a normed vector space over $\mathbb{K}\in\{\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C}\}$.

concepts.label: Bounded Linear Operator

content.statement: A bounded linear operator is a linear map between normed vector spaces whose output norm is controlled by a constant multiple of the input norm.
content.definition: A bounded linear operator is a linear operator $T:X\to Y$ such that $\|Tx\|_Y\le C\|x\|_X$ for all $x\in X$ and some constant $C\ge 0$.
content.formal: Let $(X,\|\cdot\|_X)$ and $(Y,\|\cdot\|_Y)$ be normed vector spaces. A linear map $T:X\to Y$ is bounded iff $$\exists C\ge 0\,\forall x\in X:\ \|Tx\|_Y\le C\|x\|_X.$$
content.intuition: The operator may stretch vectors, but only by one uniform linear factor. This is not the same as saying the image of all of $X$ is bounded; nonzero linear maps on unbounded normed spaces usually have unbounded image.
notation: $$T\in\mathcal{B}(X,Y)\iff T\text{ is linear and }\exists C\ge 0\ \forall x\in X:\ \|Tx\|_Y\le C\|x\|_X.$$

assumptions: $(X,\|\cdot\|_X)$ and $(Y,\|\cdot\|_Y)$ are normed vector spaces.
$T:X\to Y$ is linear.

concepts.label: Bounded Operator Space is Banach when the Codomain is Banach

content.statement: For normed spaces $X$ and $Y$, the bounded linear operators $\mathcal{B}(X,Y)$ form a normed vector space under the operator norm; if $Y$ is Banach, then $\mathcal{B}(X,Y)$ is Banach.
content.formal: Let $(X,\|\cdot\|_X)$ and $(Y,\|\cdot\|_Y)$ be normed vector spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb{K}\in\{\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C}\}$. Then $\mathcal{B}(X,Y)$, equipped with $$\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\sup_{\|x\|_X\le 1}\|Ax\|_Y,$$ is a normed vector space. If $Y$ is Banach, then $\mathcal{B}(X,Y)$ is complete in this norm.
content.intuition: A Cauchy sequence of operators is uniformly Cauchy on the unit ball. Evaluating at each vector gives Cauchy sequences in $Y$, so completeness of $Y$ supplies the pointwise limit operator and the same uniform estimate gives operator-norm convergence.
notation: $$\mathcal{B}(X,Y)=\{A:X\to Y: A \text{ is linear and bounded}\}$$

assumptions: $X$ and $Y$ are normed linear spaces over the same scalar field, usually $\mathbb{K}=\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$.
The operator norm $\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ is defined by the supremum over the unit ball of $X$.
Completeness of $\mathcal{B}(X,Y)$ requires completeness of $Y$, not of $X$.

steps.content: Let $(A_n)$ be a Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal{B}(X,Y)$ with respect to $\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{op}}$. We construct $A:X\to Y$ and prove $A_n\to A$ in operator norm.

For every $B\in\mathcal{B}(X,Y)$ and every $x\in X$, $$\|Bx\|_Y\le \|B\|_{\mathrm{op}}\,\|x\|_X.$$ For $x=0$ this is clear. For $x\ne0$, apply the definition of the operator norm to $u=x/\|x\|_X$, then use linearity.
Since $(A_n)$ is Cauchy in the normed space $\mathcal{B}(X,Y)$, there exists $M<\infty$ such that $\|A_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le M$ for all $n$.
For each fixed $x\in X$, Lemma A gives $$\|A_nx-A_mx\|_Y\le \|A_n-A_m\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|x\|_X.$$ Thus $(A_nx)$ is Cauchy in $Y$. Since $Y$ is Banach, define $$Ax=\lim_{n\to\infty}A_nx.$$

For $x,y\in X$ and $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{K}$, pass to the limit in $$A_n(\alpha x+\beta y)=\alpha A_nx+\beta A_ny.$$ The vector-space operations in $Y$ are continuous with respect to its norm, so $A(\alpha x+\beta y)=\alpha Ax+\beta Ay$.
By Lemma B and Lemma A, $$\|A_nx\|_Y\le M\|x\|_X\qquad(n\in\mathbb{N}).$$ Letting $n\to\infty$ gives $\|Ax\|_Y\le M\|x\|_X$ for every $x\in X$. Hence $A$ is bounded and $A\in\mathcal{B}(X,Y)$.

Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $N$ such that $\|A_n-A_m\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\varepsilon$ for $n,m\ge N$. For $\|x\|_X\le1$, let $m\to\infty$ in $$\|A_nx-A_mx\|_Y\le\varepsilon.$$ Then $\|A_nx-Ax\|_Y\le\varepsilon$ for every unit-ball vector $x$, so $\|A_n-A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\varepsilon$ for all $n\ge N$.

Every Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal{B}(X,Y)$ converges in operator norm to an element of $\mathcal{B}(X,Y)$. Therefore $\mathcal{B}(X,Y)$ is Banach whenever $Y$ is Banach. Completeness of $X$ is not used.

source.citation: Standard functional analysis theorem: completeness of $\mathcal{B}(X,Y)$ when $Y$ is Banach; bounded linear operators between normed spaces.

content.definition: A set or operator is bounded when its size is controlled by a finite constant in the relevant norm.
content.intuition: Uniform finite control.

content.statement: The diagonal operator $T(x_n)=(x_n/n)$ on $\ell^2$ has norm $1$, is compact, and is not invertible.
content.formal: $$T:\ell^2\to\ell^2,\qquad T(x_1,x_2,\ldots)=\left(x_1,\frac{x_2}{2},\ldots\right),\qquad \|T\|=1.$$
content.intuition: The diagonal entries tend to zero, so truncations approximate $T$ in operator norm, while the inverse would multiply coordinates by an unbounded sequence.

steps.content: $\|Tx\|_2\leq\|x\|_2$ gives $\|T\|\leq1$, while $Te_1=e_1$ gives equality.
Let $T_N$ retain only the first $N$ coordinates. Each $T_N$ has finite rank and $\|T-T_N\|=1/(N+1)\to0$, so $T$ is compact.
The vector $(1/n)$ lies in $\ell^2$, but a preimage would be $(1,1,\ldots)\notin\ell^2$. Hence $T$ is not surjective and not invertible.

content.definition: A bounded linear operator that maps bounded sets to relatively compact sets.
content.formal: $$T:X\to Y \text{ compact in } \mathcal{L}(X,Y) \quad \iff \quad T(B_X) \text{ has compact closure in } Y.$$
content.formula: $$\begin{aligned}T:X\to Y \text{ compact, means } \forall \text{ bounded } B\subseteq X,\ \overline{T(B)} \text{ is compact in } Y.\end{aligned}$$
content.intuition: An infinite-dimensional operator behaving partly like a finite-rank operator.

content.definition: A linear operator that is continuous between the given topologies.
content.intuition: The same object as a bounded linear operator in normed spaces.

concepts.label: Kernel

content.statement: The kernel of a linear operator is the set of vectors mapped to zero.
content.definition: The null space of a linear operator.
content.formal: $$\ker T=\{x\in X:Tx=0\}.$$
content.intuition: Everything the operator kills.

assumptions: $$T:X\to Y is linear.$$

content.definition: A linear operator is an operator between vector spaces that preserves addition and scalar multiplication.
content.formal: Let $X,Y$ be vector spaces over $\mathbb K$. A map $T:X\to Y$ is a linear operator iff $T(\alpha x+\beta y)=\alpha Tx+\beta Ty$ for all $x,y\in X$ and $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb K$.
content.intuition: An operator that respects superposition: transform after combining equals combine after transforming.

concepts.label: Nonlinear operator

content.statement: A nonlinear operator is an operator that is not linear.
content.definition: A nonlinear operator is a map between structured spaces that fails linearity.
content.formal: A map $F:X\to Y$ is nonlinear if there exist $x,y\in X$ or $\lambda\in\mathbb K$ such that $F(x+y)\ne F(x)+F(y)$ or $F(\lambda x)\ne \lambda F(x)$.
content.intuition: Still an operator because it acts on structured spaces; not a linear operator because it refuses to respect superposition.

assumptions: $X$ and $Y$ are structured spaces, usually vector or normed spaces.
$F:X\to Y$ is a function.
$F$ fails additivity or homogeneity.

content.statement: A map is nonlinear if it fails additivity or homogeneity.
content.definition: Failure of linearity.
content.formal: A map $F:X\to Y$ between vector spaces over $\mathbb K$ is nonlinear if linearity fails for at least one instance, i.e. $$\exists x,y\in X:\ F(x+y)\neq F(x)+F(y)\qquad\text{or}\qquad\exists x\in X,\ \lambda\in\mathbb K:\ F(\lambda x)\neq\lambda F(x).$$ Note the quantifier: nonlinearity is a single counterexample, not failure for all arguments.
content.intuition: The map does not respect superposition.

concepts.label: Nonzero linear map on unbounded normed space

content.statement: A nonzero bounded linear operator need not be bounded as a function on all of X.
content.definition: This distinguishes bounded linear operator from bounded function on its whole domain.
content.formal: $$T\ne0,\ T\in\mathcal L(X,Y) \implies \sup_{x\in X}\|Tx\|_Y=\infty.$$
content.intuition: Linear maps scale. If one vector has nonzero image, scaling that vector makes the image arbitrarily large.

assumptions: $T:X\to Y$ is linear.
$X$ is a normed vector space over an unbounded scalar field.

concepts.label: Operator

content.statement: In functional analysis, an operator is a map between structured spaces, usually vector, normed, Banach, or Hilbert spaces.
content.definition: An operator is a function or map acting between structured spaces. In functional analysis, the term usually signals that the domain and codomain are vector spaces or topological vector spaces, and often that the map is linear unless explicitly stated otherwise.
content.formal: An operator is typically a map $T:X\to Y$ where $X,Y$ carry mathematical structure; in functional analysis $X,Y$ are usually vector or normed spaces. If additionally $T(\alpha x+\beta y)=\alpha Tx+\beta Ty$, then $T$ is a linear operator.
content.intuition: A function wearing structure: it is still an assignment, but the word operator tells the reader to care about vector-space, norm, topology, or Hilbert-space structure.

assumptions: $T$ is a function/map.
The domain and codomain usually carry additional structure.
In functional analysis, linearity is common but should not be assumed unless stated or conventional in the surrounding text.

source.citation: standard functional-analysis convention; compatible with Bowers-Kalton notation L(X,Y)

content.definition: The operator norm of a bounded linear operator is its largest possible output size on the unit ball of the domain.
content.formal: Let $T:X\to Y$ be linear between normed spaces. $$\|T\|=\sup_{\|x\|_X\leq 1}\|Tx\|_Y=\sup_{x\neq 0}\frac{\|Tx\|_Y}{\|x\|_X}.$$
content.intuition: The operator norm is the worst-case stretch factor: send the domain unit ball through $T$ and measure the farthest point in the codomain norm.

concepts.label: Space of Bounded Linear Operators

content.statement: For normed spaces $X$ and $Y$, $\mathcal{B}(X,Y)$ is the vector space of bounded linear operators from $X$ to $Y$, equipped with the operator norm.
content.definition: The bounded operator space $\mathcal{B}(X,Y)$ consists of all bounded linear maps $A:X\to Y$. It is made into a normed vector space by pointwise vector operations and the operator norm.
content.formal: Let $(X,\|\cdot\|_X)$ and $(Y,\|\cdot\|_Y)$ be normed vector spaces over the same scalar field. Then $$\mathcal{B}(X,Y)=\{A:X\to Y: A\text{ is linear and }\exists C\ge0\ \forall x\in X\ \|Ax\|_Y\le C\|x\|_X\},$$ with $$\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\sup_{\|x\|_X\le1}\|Ax\|_Y.$$
content.intuition: This packages all uniformly controlled linear transformations from $X$ to $Y$ into one normed space. Addition and scalar multiplication are done operator-by-operator, while the norm measures the largest stretch on the unit ball of $X$.
notation: $\mathcal{L}(X,Y)$ when the convention identifies continuous and bounded linear maps

assumptions: $X$ and $Y$ are normed vector spaces over the same scalar field.
Operators in $\mathcal{B}(X,Y)$ are linear and bounded.
The norm on $\mathcal{B}(X,Y)$ is the operator norm.

concepts.label: Unbounded scalar multiples

content.statement: If $y\neq0$ in a normed space, then scalar multiples of $y$ have arbitrarily large norm.
content.definition: For any nonzero vector $y$ in a normed vector space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, the set $\{\lambda y:\lambda\in\mathbb K\}$ is unbounded because $\|\lambda y\|=|\lambda|\|y\|$ and $|\lambda|$ can be made arbitrarily large.
content.formal: $$y\neq0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \forall M>0\,\exists\lambda\in\mathbb K:\ \|\lambda y\|>M.$$
content.intuition: A nonzero vector determines a line through the origin. Scaling along that line eventually leaves every bounded ball.

assumptions: $(Y,\|\cdot\|_Y)$ is a normed vector space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.
$y\in Y$ and $y\neq0$.

concepts.label: Adjoint operator

content.definition: The Banach-space adjoint of $T\in\mathcal B(X,Y)$ is the operator $T^*\in\mathcal B(Y^*,X^*)$ obtained by precomposition with $T$: it sends a functional on $Y$ to a functional on $X$.
content.formal: Let $X,Y$ be normed spaces over $\mathbb K$ and $T\in\mathcal B(X,Y)$. Define $$T^*:Y^*\to X^*,\qquad T^*y^*=y^*\circ T,$$ that is, $$(T^*y^*)(x)=y^*(Tx)\qquad\text{for all }x\in X,\ y^*\in Y^*.$$ In the duality pairing $\langle x^*,x\rangle:=x^*(x)$ this reads $$\langle T^*y^*,x\rangle=\langle y^*,Tx\rangle.$$ The map $T\mapsto T^*$ is linear, and isometric: $\|T^*\|=\|T\|$.
content.intuition: Move $T$ from vectors to scalar probes by precomposition. A probe on the target becomes a probe on the source by first applying $T$ and then measuring.
content.gloss: Type discipline: $T^*$ acts on functionals, not on vectors. It goes $Y^*\to X^*$, reversing the arrow. The pairing $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ here is the bilinear duality pairing, not an inner product, and no conjugation occurs. This is a different construction from the Hilbert adjoint, which acts $Y\to X$ on vectors and is conjugate-linear in $T$.

examples.content: $\|T^*\|=\|T\|$ holds for every $T\in\mathcal B(X,Y)$. The inequality $\|T^*\|\leq\|T\|$ is direct from $|(T^*y^*)(x)|\leq\|y^*\|\|T\|\|x\|$; the reverse uses Hahn-Banach to pick a norming functional for $Tx$.
examples.label: It is isometric

examples.content: On a Hilbert space the two notions are related but not equal. The Banach adjoint is $T^*:H^*\to H^*$ and is linear in $T$; the Hilbert adjoint is $T^*:H\to H$ characterised by $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,T^*y\rangle$, and satisfies $(\lambda T)^*=\overline{\lambda}T^*$. They correspond under the Riesz map, and the conjugation appears precisely because that map is conjugate-linear.
examples.label: Contrast with the Hilbert adjoint

assumptions: $X,Y$ are normed spaces over the same field $\mathbb K$; completeness is not required.
$T$ is bounded and linear, which is what makes $y^*\circ T$ continuous.
The pairing is the duality pairing between $X^*$ and $X$, not an inner product.

concepts.label: Banach-Alaoglu Theorem

content.statement: The closed unit ball of the dual space is compact in the weak-star topology. No completeness, separability or reflexivity of $X$ is required.
content.formal: Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and let $X$ be a normed vector space over $\mathbb K$, with continuous dual $X^*=\mathcal L(X,\mathbb K)$ and closed dual unit ball $$B_{X^*}=\{x^*\in X^*:\|x^*\|_{X^*}\leq1\}.$$ Then $B_{X^*}$ is compact in the weak-star topology $\sigma(X^*,X)$, that is, $$\forall\,\mathcal U\subseteq\sigma(X^*,X)\ \text{with}\ B_{X^*}\subseteq\bigcup\mathcal U:\ \exists\,U_1,\dots,U_n\in\mathcal U\ \text{with}\ B_{X^*}\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^nU_i.$$ Equivalently, in net form: every net $(x_\alpha^*)_{\alpha\in A}$ in $B_{X^*}$ admits a subnet $(x^*_{\alpha_\beta})_\beta$ and some $x^*\in B_{X^*}$ with $$\forall x\in X:\quad x^*_{\alpha_\beta}(x)\longrightarrow x^*(x).$$ The limit $x^*$ may depend on the net and the chosen subnet, but not on $x$.
content.intuition: Elements of $B_{X^*}$ are exactly the functionals whose values are constrained pointwise: $|x^*(x)|\leq\|x\|$ for every $x$. So the ball sits inside a product of scalar discs, one disc per vector $x$, and Tychonoff makes that product compact. Weak-star is precisely the topology in which this product picture is faithful, which is why the theorem is false for the norm topology.
content.gloss: The single real idea is Tychonoff; every other step is bookkeeping about which conditions are pointwise-closed.

examples.content: Compactness genuinely requires the weak-star topology. If $\dim X^*=\infty$, then $B_{X^*}$ is not norm compact: by Riesz's lemma there is a sequence in $B_{X^*}$ with mutual distances at least $1/2$, so no norm-convergent subsequence exists. Concretely, in $\ell^1=(c_0)^*$ the basis vectors satisfy $\|e_n-e_m\|_1=2$ for $n\neq m$.
examples.label: Norm topology fails

examples.content: The result does not survive replacing $\sigma(X^*,X)$ by $\sigma(X^*,X^{**})$. By Kakutani's theorem, $B_{X^*}$ is weakly compact if and only if $X^*$ is reflexive. For $X=c_0$ the ball $B_{\ell^1}$ is weak-star compact but not weakly compact, since $\ell^1$ is not reflexive.
examples.label: Weak topology fails

examples.content: The hypothesis that the ball is closed is load-bearing. The open ball $\{x^*:\|x^*\|<1\}$ is not weak-star compact, since it is not even weak-star closed: its weak-star closure is $B_{X^*}$.
examples.label: Open ball fails

examples.content: Compactness here is the open-cover notion, and does not by itself give sequences. For $X=\ell^\infty$, which is non-separable, $B_{X^*}$ is weak-star compact yet not weak-star sequentially compact. Only when $X$ is separable is $B_{X^*}$ weak-star metrizable, giving the sequential form used in practice.
examples.label: Compact but not sequentially compact

examples.content: If $X$ is separable, $(B_{X^*},\sigma(X^*,X))$ is a compact metrizable space, so every norm-bounded sequence $(x_n^*)\subseteq X^*$ has a weak-star convergent subsequence. This is the form used to extract limits in calculus of variations and PDE.
examples.label: Separable case: the sequential corollary

examples.content: If $X$ is reflexive then $\sigma(X^*,X)=\sigma(X^*,X^{**})$, and applying the theorem to $X^*$ shows $B_X$ is weakly compact. Combined with Eberlein-Smulian this yields weak sequential compactness of bounded sets in reflexive spaces.
examples.label: Reflexive case

assumptions: $X$ is a normed vector space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Completeness of $X$ is not assumed and is not used.
$B_{X^*}$ carries the weak-star topology $\sigma(X^*,X)$, not the dual-norm topology and not $\sigma(X^*,X^{**})$.
The ball is the closed unit ball; the open ball is not weak-star compact.
Tychonoff's theorem is invoked for a product of compact Hausdorff spaces, so the ultrafilter lemma suffices and full choice is not needed.

steps.content: Let $x^*\in B_{X^*}$. By definition of the dual norm, $|x^*(x)|\leq\|x^*\|\,\|x\|\leq\|x\|$ for every $x\in X$. Hence $x^*(x)\in D_x:=\{\lambda\in\mathbb K:|\lambda|\leq\|x\|\}$, and the norm bound on the functional has been converted into a family of bounds on numbers, one for each $x$.

Define $$\Phi:B_{X^*}\to P:=\prod_{x\in X}D_x,\qquad \Phi(x^*)=(x^*(x))_{x\in X}.$$ The map $\Phi$ is well defined by the previous step and injective, since two functionals agreeing at every $x\in X$ are equal as functions.

Each $D_x\subseteq\mathbb K$ is closed and bounded, hence compact by Heine-Borel. By Tychonoff's theorem the product $P$ is compact in the product topology. This is the only nontrivial ingredient in the proof.

The product topology on $P$ is the topology of pointwise convergence on $X$, and $\sigma(X^*,X)$ is by construction the initial topology induced by the evaluations $\hat x(x^*)=x^*(x)$. These are the same family of maps, so $\Phi$ is a homeomorphism from $(B_{X^*},\sigma(X^*,X))$ onto its image $\Phi(B_{X^*})\subseteq P$ with the subspace topology.

The image is cut out by linearity, which is a pointwise condition: for fixed $x,y\in X$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb K$ the set $$C_{x,y,\lambda}=\{\varphi\in P:\varphi(x+\lambda y)-\varphi(x)-\lambda\varphi(y)=0\}$$ is closed, being the preimage of $\{0\}$ under a map continuous in the product topology (it depends on three coordinates only). Hence $$\Phi(B_{X^*})=\bigcap_{x,y\in X,\ \lambda\in\mathbb K}C_{x,y,\lambda}$$ is closed in $P$; the norm bound $\|x^*\|\leq1$ is already encoded in the discs $D_x$.
A closed subset of a compact space is compact, so $\Phi(B_{X^*})$ is compact in $P$. Transporting back through the homeomorphism $\Phi^{-1}$ shows $B_{X^*}$ is compact in $\sigma(X^*,X)$.

source.citation: Banach-Alaoglu; see also the sequential form for separable $X$ (Banach-Alaoglu-Bourbaki)

concepts.label: Canonical embedding is isometric

content.statement: Every normed space embeds linearly and isometrically into its bidual.
content.formal: For $x\in X$, define $Jx\in X^{**}$ by $(Jx)(f)=f(x)$. Then $$\|Jx\|_{X^{**}}=\sup_{\|f\|_{X^*}\leq1}|f(x)|=\|x\|_X.$$
content.intuition: The bidual records every continuous scalar measurement of a vector without losing its norm.

assumptions: $X$ is a normed vector space.
$X^*$ is the continuous dual of $X$.
$X^{**}$ is the bidual of $X$.

steps.content: For $\|f\|\leq1$, boundedness gives $|f(x)|\leq\|x\|$, hence $\|Jx\|\leq\|x\|$.
If $x\neq0$, Hahn-Banach gives $f\in X^*$ with $\|f\|=1$ and $f(x)=\|x\|$; the case $x=0$ is immediate. Thus $\|Jx\|\geq\|x\|$.

concepts.label: Closed convex sets are weakly closed

content.statement: A norm-closed convex subset of a locally convex space is closed for the weak topology induced by its continuous dual.
content.formal: $$C\text{ convex and closed}\Longrightarrow C\text{ is }\sigma(X,X^*)\text{-closed}.$$
content.intuition: Continuous linear functionals separate every exterior point, so weak limits cannot escape a closed convex set.

assumptions: $X$ is a locally convex space.
$C\subset X$ is a convex set.

steps.content: If $x\notin C$, a separation theorem gives a weakly continuous functional whose value at $x$ is strictly separated from all values on $C$.
The inverse image of the separating scalar neighborhood is weakly open, contains $x$, and misses $C$. Thus the weak complement of $C$ is open.

concepts.label: Dual norm geometry

content.statement: The dual norm measures the largest scalar reading a functional can take on the unit ball.
content.definition: For a continuous linear functional $x^*\in X^*$, its norm is the support value of the unit ball in the direction $x^*$.
content.intuition: A functional is a scalar probe. Its norm is the farthest signed level it can see while the input vector stays inside the unit ball.

assumptions: $X$ is a normed vector space.
$x^*\in X^*$ is continuous and linear.

content.definition: The dual space of a normed vector space is the normed space of all continuous linear functionals on it, equipped with the operator norm.
content.formal: Let $(X,\|\cdot\|)$ be a normed vector space over $\mathbb{K}$. Its dual space is $X^*:=\mathcal{B}(X,\mathbb{K})$, the space of bounded linear functionals on $X$, equipped with the operator norm $\|f\|=\sup_{\|x\|\le 1}|f(x)|$.
content.formula: $$\begin{aligned} X^* &:= \mathcal{B}(X,\mathbb{K}) \\ &= \{f:X\to\mathbb{K}: f\text{ is linear and bounded}\}, \\ \|f\|_{X^*} &:= \sup_{\|x\|\le 1}|f(x)|=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{|f(x)|}{\|x\|}. \end{aligned}$$
content.intuition: The dual space contains the continuous linear scalar measurements of vectors in $X$; its norm records the largest size such a measurement can have on the unit ball of $X$.

concepts.label: Dual Space is Banach

content.statement: For every normed vector space $X$ over $\mathbb{K}\in\{\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C}\}$, the dual space $X^*$ is a Banach space.
content.formal: Let $(X,\|\cdot\|_X)$ be a normed vector space over $\mathbb{K}\in\{\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C}\}$. Then $$X^*=\mathcal{B}(X,\mathbb{K})$$ is complete under the operator norm $$\|f\|=\sup_{\|x\|_X\le 1}|f(x)|.$$
content.intuition: The dual is a special case of the theorem that bounded operators into a Banach codomain form a Banach space. The domain $X$ need only be normed; completeness comes from the scalar codomain $\mathbb{K}$.

assumptions: $X$ is a normed vector space.
$\mathbb{K}\in\{\mathbb{R},\mathbb{C}\}$.
$\mathbb{K}$ is Banach under its usual absolute-value norm.

steps.content: By definition, $X^*=\mathcal{B}(X,\mathbb{K})$, the space of bounded linear maps from $X$ into the scalar field.
The scalar field $\mathbb{K}$ is complete under the absolute-value norm, so it is a Banach space.
Since bounded linear operators into a Banach space form a Banach space under the operator norm, $\mathcal{B}(X,\mathbb{K})$ is Banach.
Therefore $X^*$ is Banach.

concepts.label: Dual unit ball with weak-star topology

content.statement: The closed unit ball of $X^*$ is considered with the weak-star topology $\sigma(X^*,X)$, not with the dual-norm topology and not with $\sigma(X^*,X^{**})$.
content.formal: $$B_{X^*}=\{x^*\in X^*:\|x^*\|_{X^*}\leq1\}\quad\text{equipped with}\quad\sigma(X^*,X).$$ Three distinct topologies are available on $X^*$, ordered by fineness: $$\sigma(X^*,X)\ \subseteq\ \sigma(X^*,X^{**})\ \subseteq\ \mathcal T_{\|\cdot\|_{X^*}}.$$ Banach-Alaoglu asserts compactness of $B_{X^*}$ in the coarsest of the three, and is false in the other two whenever $\dim X^*=\infty$.
content.intuition: Banach-Alaoglu is a compactness theorem for one specific topology, and the hypothesis is doing real work: compactness is bought by weakening the topology until the ball fits inside a product of scalar discs. The closedness of the ball matters too, since the open ball is not even weak-star closed.

assumptions: $X$ is a normed vector space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$; completeness is not required.
The ball is closed, i.e. $\|x^*\|\leq1$ rather than $\|x^*\|<1$.
A distinguished predual $X$ is fixed, since $\sigma(X^*,X)$ depends on it.

content.definition: Translate a problem about vectors or operators into a problem about linear functionals or adjoints.
content.intuition: Probe objects by scalar-valued tests.

concepts.label: Duality of $L^p$ spaces

content.statement: For conjugate exponents with $1\leq p<\infty$, the dual of $L^p$ is isometrically isomorphic to $L^q$, with functionals given by integration against a function.
content.formal: Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a $\sigma$-finite measure space, $1\leq p<\infty$, and let $q$ be the conjugate exponent, $$\frac1p+\frac1q=1,\qquad q=\infty\ \text{when}\ p=1.$$ Then the map $$\Lambda:L^q(\mu)\to L^p(\mu)^*,\qquad (\Lambda g)(f)=\int_\Omega f\,\overline{g}\,d\mu,$$ is a bijective isometry, so $$L^p(\mu)^*\cong L^q(\mu),\qquad\|\Lambda g\|_{(L^p)^*}=\|g\|_q.$$ For sequence spaces this reads $(\ell^p)^*\cong\ell^q$.
content.intuition: Every continuous probe on $L^p$ is integration against a function from the conjugate space, and Holder's inequality is exactly the statement that such integration is bounded. The exponent $q$ is forced: it is the unique one making the pairing bounded for all $f$.
content.gloss: The case $p=q=2$ is the Riesz representation theorem for the Hilbert space $L^2$, the one point where the space is its own dual.

examples.content: The theorem requires $p<\infty$. It is false that $(L^\infty)^*\cong L^1$: the dual of $L^\infty$ is strictly larger, containing functionals such as a Banach limit or, on $\ell^\infty$, extensions of the limit functional from $c$ obtained by Hahn-Banach, which are not given by any $\ell^1$ sequence. Consequently $(\ell^1)^*\cong\ell^\infty$ holds while $(\ell^\infty)^*\cong\ell^1$ fails, and this asymmetry is why $\ell^1$ is not reflexive.
examples.label: $p=\infty$ is excluded

examples.content: Applying the theorem twice gives $(L^p)^{**}\cong(L^q)^*\cong L^p$, and the composite is the canonical embedding, so $L^p$ is reflexive for $1<p<\infty$. It fails for $p=1$ and $p=\infty$, which is exactly why bounded sequences in $L^1$ need not have weakly convergent subsequences.
examples.label: Reflexivity for $1<p<\infty$

examples.content: For $p=1$ the hypothesis of $\sigma$-finiteness is needed: on a non-$\sigma$-finite measure space $(L^1)^*$ can be strictly larger than $L^\infty$. For $1<p<\infty$ the result holds without it.
examples.label: $\sigma$-finiteness

assumptions: $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ is a measure space, $\sigma$-finite when $p=1$.
$1\leq p<\infty$; the case $p=\infty$ is genuinely excluded.
