$q$ is the conjugate exponent defined by $1/p+1/q=1$.

concepts.label: Eberlein-Smulian Theorem

content.statement: For subsets of a Banach space, weak compactness is equivalent to weak sequential compactness.
content.formal: $K\subseteq X$ is relatively weakly compact if and only if every sequence in $K$ has a weakly convergent subsequence with limit in $\overline K^{\,w}$.
content.intuition: Although the weak topology need not be metrizable, sequences still detect its compactness on Banach spaces.

assumptions: $X$ is a Banach space.
$K\subseteq X$.

concepts.label: Goldstine's Theorem

content.statement: The canonical image of the closed unit ball of a normed space is weak-star dense in the closed unit ball of its bidual.
content.formal: Let $X$ be a normed space, $J:X\to X^{**}$ the canonical embedding. Then $$\overline{J(B_X)}^{\,\sigma(X^{**},X^*)}=B_{X^{**}}.$$ Explicitly: for every $x^{**}\in B_{X^{**}}$, every finite set $x_1^*,\dots,x_n^*\in X^*$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, there exists $x\in B_X$ with $$|x_i^*(x)-x^{**}(x_i^*)|<\varepsilon\qquad\text{for }i=1,\dots,n.$$ The vector $x$ may depend on all of $x^{**}$, the finitely many probes, and $\varepsilon$.
content.intuition: Vectors in $X$ approximate bidual vectors on every finite collection of dual probes. Density is only weak-star, so no single $x\in B_X$ works for all probes at once unless $X$ is reflexive; the finiteness of the probe set is what makes the approximation possible.
content.gloss: Pairs with Alaoglu in the standard reflexivity argument: Alaoglu makes $J(B_X)$ closed once it is compact, Goldstine makes it dense, and closed plus dense gives equality.

examples.content: In $X=c_0$ we have $X^{**}=\ell^\infty$, and $J(B_{c_0})$ is weak-star dense in $B_{\ell^\infty}$. But $J(c_0)=c_0$ is norm closed in $\ell^\infty$ and proper, so $\mathbf 1=(1,1,\dots)\in B_{\ell^\infty}$ is at norm distance $1$ from $J(B_{c_0})$. Approximation holds on finitely many probes only.
examples.label: Density is not norm density

examples.content: If $J(B_X)$ happens to be weak-star compact, hence closed, Goldstine upgrades density to equality $J(B_X)=B_{X^{**}}$, which is surjectivity of $J$ on balls and therefore reflexivity.
examples.label: Use in the reflexivity criterion

assumptions: $X$ is a normed vector space; completeness is not required.
$X^*$ is the continuous dual and $X^{**}$ the bidual.
The closure is taken in $\sigma(X^{**},X^*)$, the weak-star topology of $X^{**}$ over the predual $X^*$.

content.definition: A linear map from a vector space to its scalar field.
content.formal: Let $X$ be a vector space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. A linear functional is a map $f:X\to\mathbb K$ satisfying $$f(x+\lambda y)=f(x)+\lambda f(y)\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in X,\ \lambda\in\mathbb K.$$ If $X$ is normed, $f$ is continuous if and only if it is bounded, i.e. $$\exists C\in[0,\infty)\ \forall x\in X:\quad|f(x)|\leq C\|x\|,$$ and the set of such $f$ is the continuous dual $X^*=\mathcal L(X,\mathbb K)$.
content.intuition: A scalar measurement of vectors.

content.definition: A normed space is reflexive when its canonical embedding into the bidual is surjective.
content.formal: $$X\text{ reflexive}\iff J(X)=X^{**}.$$
content.intuition: Every continuous functional on the dual is evaluation at a vector of the original space.

concepts.label: Riesz Representation Theorem for C(K)

content.statement: Every continuous linear functional on $C(K)$ is integration against a unique regular Borel measure, isometrically.
content.formal: Let $K$ be a compact Hausdorff space and $C(K)$ the space of continuous $\mathbb K$-valued functions with the supremum norm. Then $$C(K)^*\cong M(K),$$ where $M(K)$ is the space of regular Borel measures on $K$ of finite total variation: every $\varphi\in C(K)^*$ is represented by a unique $\mu\in M(K)$ via $$\varphi(f)=\int_K f\,d\mu\qquad\text{for all }f\in C(K),$$ and the correspondence is isometric, $$\|\varphi\|_{C(K)^*}=|\mu|(K).$$
content.intuition: Every continuous scalar probe on $C(K)$ is integration against a measure. Where the Hilbert version identifies the dual with the space itself, here the dual is a genuinely different object: functions in, measures out. The norm of the functional is the total mass of the measure.
content.gloss: Type discipline: $f\in C(K)$ is a function, $\varphi\in C(K)^*$ is a functional, $\mu\in M(K)$ is a measure, and $|\mu|(K)$ is a number. The theorem is an isometric isomorphism between the second and third of these.

examples.content: For $t\in K$ the evaluation functional $\varphi(f)=f(t)$ is continuous with $\|\varphi\|=1$, and corresponds to the Dirac measure $\delta_t$, since $\int_Kf\,d\delta_t=f(t)$ and $|\delta_t|(K)=1$.
examples.label: Point evaluation is a Dirac measure

examples.content: Without restricting to regular measures the correspondence is not injective: on a non-metrizable compact Hausdorff space distinct Borel measures can integrate all continuous functions identically. Regularity, i.e. inner approximation by compacts and outer approximation by opens, is what pins down $\mu$ uniquely. When $K$ is compact metric every finite Borel measure is automatically regular, which is why the hypothesis is invisible in the Bowers-Kalton version.
examples.label: Regularity is needed for uniqueness

examples.content: Combining with Banach-Alaoglu: for $K$ compact metric, $C(K)$ is separable, so $B_{M(K)}$ is weak-star compact and metrizable. Every sequence of probability measures on $K$ therefore has a subsequence converging weak-star, which is Prokhorov-type compactness obtained purely by duality.
examples.label: Source of weak-star compactness for measures

examples.content: For $K=[0,1]$ the bidual $C(K)^{**}=M(K)^*$ is strictly larger than $C(K)$, since $M(K)$ contains $\delta_t$ for every $t$ and $M(K)^*$ contains functionals not given by continuous functions. So $C[0,1]$ is a standard non-reflexive space, and bounded sequences in it need not have weakly convergent subsequences.
examples.label: $C(K)$ is not reflexive

assumptions: $K$ is a compact Hausdorff space; in the Bowers-Kalton version $K$ is compact metric, where regularity is automatic.
$C(K)$ carries the supremum norm $\|f\|_\infty=\sup_{t\in K}|f(t)|$.
$M(K)$ consists of regular Borel measures of finite total variation, normed by $\|\mu\|=|\mu|(K)$.
Regularity is required for uniqueness of the representing measure.

concepts.label: Sequential criterion for reflexivity

content.statement: A Banach space is reflexive if and only if every norm-bounded sequence has a weakly convergent subsequence.
content.formal: Let $X$ be a Banach space. Then $$X\ \text{reflexive}\iff\forall(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\subseteq X\ \text{with}\ \sup_n\|x_n\|<\infty:\ \exists\ \text{subsequence}\ (x_{n_k})\ \exists x\in X:\ x_{n_k}\rightharpoonup x.$$ Reflexivity means the canonical embedding $J:X\to X^{**}$, $(Jx)(x^*)=x^*(x)$, is surjective. Completeness of $X$ is essential: $J$ is an isometry, so a reflexive space is isometrically isomorphic to the Banach space $X^{**}$ and hence complete.
content.intuition: Reflexivity turns norm-bounded sets into weakly compact sets, and on a Banach space weak compactness can be read off sequences. The forward direction is Alaoglu transported down through $J$; the reverse rebuilds surjectivity of $J$ from Goldstine density.
content.gloss: Note the asymmetry: reflexivity is a statement about $J$ being onto, not merely about $X$ and $X^{**}$ being isomorphic. James constructed a non-reflexive space isometrically isomorphic to its bidual.

examples.content: The criterion is stated for Banach spaces and the reverse direction needs it: reflexivity implies $X\cong X^{**}$ isometrically, and $X^{**}$ is complete as a dual space, so a reflexive normed space is automatically Banach. An incomplete normed space can therefore never be reflexive, whatever its sequences do.
examples.label: Completeness is load-bearing

examples.content: In $c_0$ the sequence of partial-sum vectors is bounded with no weakly convergent subsequence; likewise in $\ell^1$, where by Schur's property weak and norm convergence of sequences coincide, so a weakly convergent subsequence of $(e_n)$ would have to be norm convergent, which is impossible since $\|e_n-e_m\|_1=2$. Both spaces are thus non-reflexive.
examples.label: The standard non-reflexive examples

examples.content: These are reflexive, so every bounded sequence has a weakly convergent subsequence. For $p=1$ and $p=\infty$ reflexivity fails, which is exactly why $L^1$ and $L^\infty$ are awkward in variational problems.
examples.label: $\ell^p$ for $1<p<\infty$

assumptions: $X$ is a Banach space; completeness is used and cannot be dropped.
Reflexivity means surjectivity of the canonical $J$, not abstract isomorphism $X\cong X^{**}$.

steps.content: Assume $X$ reflexive. Applying Banach-Alaoglu to the dual of $X^*$ gives that $B_{X^{**}}$ is $\sigma(X^{**},X^*)$-compact. Since $J(X)=X^{**}$, the topology $\sigma(X^{**},X^*)$ pulls back along the isometry $J$ to $\sigma(X,X^*)$, so $B_X$ is weakly compact.

A norm-bounded sequence lies in $rB_X$ for some $r>0$, which is weakly compact by the previous step. Eberlein-Smulian converts weak compactness into weak sequential compactness on a Banach space, yielding a weakly convergent subsequence with limit in $X$.
Assume every bounded sequence has a weakly convergent subsequence. Then $B_X$ is weakly sequentially compact, so weakly compact by Eberlein-Smulian.

The map $J$ is a homeomorphism from $(X,\sigma(X,X^*))$ onto $(J(X),\sigma(X^{**},X^*))$, since both topologies are induced by the same family of probes $x^*\in X^*$. Hence $J(B_X)$ is $\sigma(X^{**},X^*)$-compact, therefore closed in the Hausdorff space $(X^{**},\sigma(X^{**},X^*))$.

Goldstine's theorem gives $\overline{J(B_X)}^{\,\sigma(X^{**},X^*)}=B_{X^{**}}$. Since $J(B_X)$ is already closed in that topology, $J(B_X)=B_{X^{**}}$. Scaling by $r>0$ gives $J(rB_X)=rB_{X^{**}}$, and every element of $X^{**}$ lies in some $rB_{X^{**}}$, so $J$ is surjective and $X$ is reflexive.

concepts.label: Weak boundedness equals norm boundedness in Banach spaces

content.statement: In a Banach space, every weakly bounded set is norm bounded.
content.formal: Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let $X$ be a normed vector space over $\mathbb K$, and let $A\subseteq X$. Suppose that $$\forall x^*\in X^*\;\exists C\in[0,\infty)\; \forall a\in A, \qquad|x^*(a)|\le C.$$ Then $$\exists M\in[0,\infty) \forall a\in A,\qquad\|a\|_X\le M.$$Here $X^*=\mathcal L(X,\mathbb K)$ denotes the continuous dual of $X$.
content.intuition: If every scalar probe sees boundedness, completeness upgrades this to actual norm boundedness.

assumptions: $X$ is Banach.
$A$ is weakly bounded.

steps.content: For each $a\in A$, define $T_a:X^*\to\mathbb K$ by $T_a(x^*)=x^*(a)$.
Weak boundedness of $A$ says that for every fixed $x^*\in X^*$, the set $\{|T_a(x^*)|:a\in A\}$ is bounded.
Since $X^*$ is Banach, the uniform boundedness principle gives $$\sup_{a\in A}\|T_a\|<\infty.$$
By the Hahn-Banach norming functional argument, $\|T_a\|=\|a\|$ for each $a\in A$.
Therefore $$\sup_{a\in A}\|a\|<\infty,$$ so $A$ is norm bounded.

concepts.label: Weak compactness results

content.statement: Banach-Alaoglu is the compactness source behind weak and weak-star compactness arguments: it supplies limit points for bounded families of functionals, and the standard results in the area are obtained by transporting it along the canonical embedding.
content.formal: The cluster of results built on $B_{X^*}$ being $\sigma(X^*,X)$-compact: $$\begin{aligned}&\text{(i) Banach-Alaoglu:} && B_{X^*}\ \text{is}\ \sigma(X^*,X)\text{-compact for every normed }X.\\ &\text{(ii) Kakutani:} && B_X\ \text{is}\ \sigma(X,X^*)\text{-compact}\iff X\ \text{is reflexive}.\\ &\text{(iii) Eberlein-Smulian:} && \text{for }K\subseteq X\ \text{Banach, weak compactness}\iff\text{weak sequential compactness}.\\ &\text{(iv) separable case:} && X\ \text{separable}\implies(B_{X^*},\sigma(X^*,X))\ \text{is compact metrizable}.\end{aligned}$$
content.intuition: Compactness appears after weakening the topology. In infinite dimensions the norm-closed unit ball is never compact, so every compactness statement in Banach space theory is bought by trading the norm topology for a coarser one; Alaoglu is the cheapest such trade because it needs no hypothesis on $X$ at all.
content.gloss: Route to remember: Alaoglu gives compactness upstairs in $X^{**}$; reflexivity is what lets you pull it back down to $X$.

examples.content: For $K$ compact metric, $C(K)$ is separable and $C(K)^*\cong M(K)$. A sequence of probability measures $(\mu_n)$ lies in $B_{M(K)}$, so by the separable case there is a subsequence and a $\mu\in B_{M(K)}$ with $\int f\,d\mu_{n_k}\to\int f\,d\mu$ for every $f\in C(K)$. This is exactly weak-star convergence of measures.
examples.label: Extracting a limit from a bounded sequence of measures

examples.content: If $X$ is reflexive and $(x_n)$ is norm bounded, then Alaoglu applied to $X^*$ plus $J(X)=X^{**}$ makes $B_X$ weakly compact, and Eberlein-Smulian converts this to a weakly convergent subsequence. This is the standard existence step in the direct method of the calculus of variations.
examples.label: Reflexive spaces: bounded sequences have weakly convergent subsequences

examples.content: By Riesz's lemma, $B_X$ is norm compact if and only if $\dim X<\infty$. So no amount of hypotheses on an infinite-dimensional $X$ will make the norm-closed unit ball compact; weakening the topology is not a convenience but the only available move.
examples.label: Why the norm topology is never an option

assumptions: $X$ is a normed vector space; individual results in the cluster add completeness or separability as indicated.

concepts.label: Weak convergence

content.statement: A sequence $(x_n)$ in $X$ converges weakly to $x\in X$ if the scalars $x^*(x_n)$ converge to $x^*(x)$ for every continuous linear functional $x^*\in X^*$. The limit $x$ is a single vector required to work for all probes simultaneously.
content.definition: Weak convergence $x_n\rightharpoonup x$ means convergence of the sequence $(x_n)$ to $x$ in the weak topology $\sigma(X,X^*)$.
content.formal: Let $X$ be a normed vector space over $\mathbb K$, let $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\subseteq X$ and let $x\in X$. Then $$x_n\rightharpoonup x\quad:\Longleftrightarrow\quad\forall x^*\in X^*:\ \lim_{n\to\infty}x^*(x_n)=x^*(x).$$ Unfolding the scalar limit, $$\exists x\in X\ \forall x^*\in X^*\ \forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists N\in\mathbb N\ \forall n\geq N:\quad|x^*(x_n)-x^*(x)|<\varepsilon.$$ The vector $x$ is quantified outside $x^*$, so it may not depend on the probe; the index $N$ is quantified inside and may depend on both $x^*$ and $\varepsilon$.
content.intuition: Vectors converge when every scalar probe in the dual agrees that they converge, and all probes agree on the same limiting vector. Weak convergence tests $x_n$ against $X^*$ one functional at a time, with no uniformity in $x^*$ required.
content.gloss: Contrast with norm convergence, which is uniformity over the whole dual ball: $\|x_n-x\|=\sup_{\|x^*\|\leq1}|x^*(x_n-x)|$.

examples.content: If $\|x_n-x\|\to0$ then $|x^*(x_n)-x^*(x)|\leq\|x^*\|\,\|x_n-x\|\to0$ for every $x^*$, so $x_n\rightharpoonup x$. The converse fails: in $\ell^2$, $e_n\rightharpoonup 0$ while $\|e_n-0\|_2=1$.
examples.label: Norm convergence is strictly stronger

examples.content: From $x_n\rightharpoonup x$ one gets $\|x\|\leq\liminf_n\|x_n\|$, but not $\|x_n\|\to\|x\|$. In $\ell^2$ with $e_n\rightharpoonup0$ the inequality is strict: $0=\|0\|<\liminf\|e_n\|=1$. In a Hilbert space, $x_n\rightharpoonup x$ together with $\|x_n\|\to\|x\|$ does upgrade to norm convergence (the Radon-Riesz property).
examples.label: The norm is only weakly lower semicontinuous

examples.content: If $x_n\rightharpoonup x$ then $\{x_n:n\in\mathbb N\}$ is weakly bounded, since each $(x^*(x_n))_n$ converges and is therefore a bounded scalar sequence. Uniform boundedness applied in $X^*$ (which is Banach regardless of $X$) then gives $\sup_n\|x_n\|<\infty$.
examples.label: Weakly convergent sequences are bounded

assumptions: $X$ is a normed vector space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.
Weak limits are unique, since $\sigma(X,X^*)$ is Hausdorff by Hahn-Banach.

concepts.label: Weak topology

content.definition: The weak topology on $X$, written $\sigma(X,X^*)$, is the coarsest topology on $X$ for which every $x^*\in X^*$ remains continuous. Equivalently, it is the initial topology induced by the family of maps $\{x^*:X\to\mathbb K\}_{x^*\in X^*}$.
content.formal: Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and let $X$ be a normed vector space over $\mathbb K$ with continuous dual $X^*=\mathcal L(X,\mathbb K)$. The weak topology is $$\sigma(X,X^*)=\bigcap\{\mathcal T:\mathcal T\text{ a topology on }X\text{ with }x^*\in C(X,\mathbb K)\ \forall x^*\in X^*\}.$$ A subbase is given by the preimages $$S=\{(x^*)^{-1}(U):x^*\in X^*,\ U\subseteq\mathbb K\text{ open}\},$$ so a base of neighbourhoods of $x_0\in X$ consists of the finite intersections $$V(x_0;x_1^*,\dots,x_n^*;\varepsilon)=\{x\in X:|x_i^*(x-x_0)|<\varepsilon\ \text{for } i=1,\dots,n\},$$ indexed by $n\in\mathbb N$, $x_1^*,\dots,x_n^*\in X^*$ and $\varepsilon>0$. Equivalently $\sigma(X,X^*)$ is the locally convex topology generated by the seminorms $$p_{x^*}(x)=|x^*(x)|,\qquad x^*\in X^*.$$
content.intuition: The weak topology keeps only the information detected by continuous linear functionals: two vectors are close when finitely many scalar probes $x^*\in X^*$ give nearly the same value on them. Only finitely many probes appear in any one basic neighbourhood, which is exactly why the topology is coarser than the norm topology.
content.gloss: Basic weak neighbourhoods constrain finitely many coordinates at a time, so they are unbounded in infinitely many directions.

examples.content: Every linear functional on a finite-dimensional normed space is continuous, and a base of weak neighbourhoods of $0$ obtained from a dual basis $e_1^*,\dots,e_n^*$ is a box around $0$. Hence $$\sigma(\mathbb R^n,(\mathbb R^n)^*)=\mathcal T_{\text{Euclidean}},$$ and weak convergence coincides with coordinatewise, hence norm, convergence.
examples.label: Finite-dimensional case

examples.content: In $\ell^2$ the standard basis satisfies $e_n\rightharpoonup 0$ by Bessel's inequality, while $\|e_n\|_2=1$ for all $n$. So $\sigma(X,X^*)$ is strictly coarser than the norm topology, and the norm is not weakly continuous.
examples.label: Infinite-dimensional case

examples.content: If $\dim X=\infty$, every weakly open $V\ni 0$ contains an infinite-dimensional subspace: with $V\supseteq V(0;x_1^*,\dots,x_n^*;\varepsilon)$, the subspace $\bigcap_{i=1}^n\ker x_i^*$ has codimension at most $n$, hence is nontrivial, and lies in $V$. Consequently no weakly open set is norm bounded, and the weak topology is not induced by any norm.
examples.label: Weak neighbourhoods are never norm bounded

examples.content: For $\dim X=\infty$ the topology $\sigma(X,X^*)$ is not metrizable on all of $X$, since a countable neighbourhood base at $0$ would involve countably many functionals and the argument above would then produce a norm-bounded weak neighbourhood. Metrizability can still hold on norm-bounded subsets, provided $X^*$ is separable.
examples.label: Not metrizable

assumptions: $X$ is a normed vector space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.
$X^*$ denotes the continuous dual $\mathcal L(X,\mathbb K)$, not the algebraic dual.
properties: Locally convex and translation invariant; $(X,\sigma(X,X^*))$ is a topological vector space.
Hausdorff, because $X^*$ separates points of $X$ (a consequence of Hahn-Banach).
Coarser than the norm topology, with equality if and only if $\dim X<\infty$.
Agrees with the norm topology on convex sets in the sense that norm-closed convex sets are weakly closed.

concepts.label: Weak-null preserving maps are bounded

content.statement: A linear map between Banach spaces that sends every weakly null sequence to a weakly null sequence is bounded.
content.formal: Let $X,Y$ be Banach spaces over $\mathbb K$ and let $T:X\to Y$ be linear. Suppose $$\forall(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\subseteq X:\quad x_n\rightharpoonup0\ \Longrightarrow\ Tx_n\rightharpoonup0.$$ Then $T\in\mathcal B(X,Y)$, that is, $$\exists C\in[0,\infty)\ \forall x\in X:\quad\|Tx\|_Y\leq C\|x\|_X.$$
content.intuition: An unbounded map can amplify a norm-null sequence into an unbounded one, but weakly convergent sequences must be norm bounded. Rescaling turns the failure of boundedness into a norm-null sequence whose image is unbounded, contradicting that hypothesis.
content.gloss: The move is: unboundedness gives a badly behaved sequence, rescale it to be null, then let the hypothesis and weak boundedness collide.

examples.content: The upgrade from weak boundedness to norm boundedness uses the uniform boundedness principle, which needs a Banach space. Completeness of $X$ is not used anywhere in the argument above, so the theorem holds for $X$ merely normed.
examples.label: Completeness of $Y$ is load-bearing

examples.content: The converse direction is elementary: if $T\in\mathcal B(X,Y)$ and $x_n\rightharpoonup0$, then for $y^*\in Y^*$ the composition $y^*\circ T$ lies in $X^*$, so $y^*(Tx_n)=(y^*\circ T)(x_n)\to0$, giving $Tx_n\rightharpoonup0$. Hence the stated condition characterises boundedness.
examples.label: Weak-to-weak continuity is automatic for bounded maps

assumptions: $Y$ is Banach; this is what licenses uniform boundedness.
$T$ is linear; the rescaling step uses homogeneity.
$X$ is normed. Completeness of $X$ is not needed for this argument.

steps.content: Suppose $T\notin\mathcal B(X,Y)$. Then $\sup_{\|y\|\leq1}\|Ty\|=\infty$, so for every $n\in\mathbb N$ there is $y_n\in X$ with $\|y_n\|=1$ and $\|Ty_n\|>n^2$.
Set $x_n=y_n/n$. Then $\|x_n\|=1/n\to0$, so $x_n\to0$ in norm, and hence $x_n\rightharpoonup0$ since $|x^*(x_n)|\leq\|x^*\|\,\|x_n\|\to0$ for each $x^*\in X^*$.
By hypothesis $Tx_n\rightharpoonup0$ in $Y$. In particular $\{Tx_n:n\in\mathbb N\}$ is weakly bounded, since each scalar sequence $(y^*(Tx_n))_n$ converges and is therefore bounded.
Since $Y$ is Banach, weak boundedness implies norm boundedness, so $\sup_n\|Tx_n\|<\infty$.
But by linearity $\|Tx_n\|=\|Ty_n\|/n>n^2/n=n\to\infty$, contradicting the previous step. Hence $T$ is bounded.

concepts.label: Weak-star convergence

content.statement: A sequence of functionals $(x_n^*)$ converges weak-star to $x^*$ if for every vector $x\in X$ the scalars $x_n^*(x)$ converge to $x^*(x)$. The limit functional $x^*$ is one object required to work at every $x$ simultaneously.
content.definition: Weak-star convergence $x_n^*\overset{w^*}{\to}x^*$ means convergence of the sequence $(x_n^*)$ to $x^*$ in the weak-star topology $\sigma(X^*,X)$, that is, pointwise convergence of functions on $X$.
content.formal: Let $X$ be a normed vector space over $\mathbb K$, let $(x_n^*)_{n\in\mathbb N}\subseteq X^*$ and let $x^*\in X^*$. Then $$x_n^*\overset{w^*}{\to}x^*\quad:\Longleftrightarrow\quad\forall x\in X:\ \lim_{n\to\infty}x_n^*(x)=x^*(x).$$ Fully unfolded, $$\exists x^*\in X^*\ \forall x\in X\ \forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists N\in\mathbb N\ \forall n\geq N:\quad|x_n^*(x)-x^*(x)|<\varepsilon.$$ The functional $x^*$ is quantified outside $x$, so it may not depend on the test vector; $N$ may depend on both $x$ and $\varepsilon$, which is precisely the absence of uniformity that distinguishes this from dual-norm convergence.
content.intuition: Functionals converge by agreeing pointwise on every vector. Weak-star convergence is the same notion as pointwise convergence of functions, transported into $X^*$.
content.gloss: Dual-norm convergence is the uniform version of the same statement: $\|x_n^*-x^*\|=\sup_{\|x\|\leq1}|x_n^*(x)-x^*(x)|\to0$, i.e. $N$ chosen independently of $x$ in the unit ball.

examples.content: In $X=c_0$ with $X^*=\ell^1$, the partial-sum functionals or the basis vectors $e_n\in\ell^1$ satisfy $e_n\overset{w^*}{\to}0$ while $\|e_n\|_1=1$. Pointwise decay at each fixed $x\in c_0$ does not force decay of the norm.
examples.label: Weak-star limits need not be norm limits

examples.content: Since $\hat X\subseteq X^{**}$, testing against all of $X^{**}$ is a stronger demand than testing against $\hat X$: $$x_n^*\rightharpoonup x^*\ \text{in }X^*\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x_n^*\overset{w^*}{\to}x^*.$$ The converse holds for all sequences exactly when $X$ is reflexive; $e_n\in\ell^1=(c_0)^*$ is the standard counterexample.
examples.label: Weak convergence implies weak-star, not conversely

examples.content: Banach-Alaoglu gives compactness of $B_{X^*}$, not sequential compactness. For non-separable $X$ such as $\ell^\infty$, $B_{X^*}$ is weak-star compact but not weak-star sequentially compact, so a bounded sequence of functionals need have no weak-star convergent subsequence; one must pass to subnets. For separable $X$, $B_{X^*}$ is weak-star metrizable and subsequences do suffice.
examples.label: Sequences do not suffice in general

assumptions: $X$ is a normed vector space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.
Weak-star limits are unique, since $\sigma(X^*,X)$ is Hausdorff.

The limit is asserted to lie in $X^*$; pointwise limits of linear maps are linear, but boundedness of the limit requires either a norm bound on the sequence or completeness of $X$ via uniform boundedness.

concepts.label: Weak-star topology

content.definition: The weak-star topology $\sigma(X^*,X)$ is the coarsest topology on $X^*$ making every evaluation map $\hat x:X^*\to\mathbb K$, $\hat x(x^*)=x^*(x)$, continuous, as $x$ ranges over $X$. It is the topology of pointwise convergence on the predual $X$.
content.formal: Let $X$ be a normed vector space over $\mathbb K$ and $X^*=\mathcal L(X,\mathbb K)$. For $x\in X$ define the evaluation functional $$\hat x:X^*\to\mathbb K,\qquad \hat x(x^*)=x^*(x).$$ Then $$\sigma(X^*,X)=\text{the initial topology on }X^*\text{ induced by }\{\hat x:x\in X\},$$ with subbase $\{\hat x^{-1}(U):x\in X,\ U\subseteq\mathbb K\text{ open}\}$ and basic neighbourhoods $$V(x_0^*;x_1,\dots,x_n;\varepsilon)=\{x^*\in X^*:|(x^*-x_0^*)(x_i)|<\varepsilon\ \text{for } i=1,\dots,n\},$$ for $n\in\mathbb N$, $x_1,\dots,x_n\in X$, $\varepsilon>0$. Equivalently it is generated by the seminorms $q_x(x^*)=|x^*(x)|$, $x\in X$.
content.intuition: Pointwise convergence on the predual $X$. Each vector $x\in X$ is reinterpreted one level up as a coordinate function $\hat x$ on $X^*$, and the weak-star topology is the product-style topology those coordinates generate.
content.gloss: Same recipe as the weak topology, applied one level up: $\sigma(X,X^*)$ probes $X$ by $X^*$, while $\sigma(X^*,X)$ probes $X^*$ by the image $\hat X\subseteq X^{**}$ only.

examples.content: The dual $X^*$ carries two probe topologies: $\sigma(X^*,X^{**})$ (its own weak topology) and $\sigma(X^*,X)$ (weak-star). Since the canonical embedding gives $\hat X\subseteq X^{**}$, fewer probes are available for weak-star, so $$\sigma(X^*,X)\subseteq\sigma(X^*,X^{**}),$$ with equality if and only if $X$ is reflexive.
examples.label: Weak-star versus weak on $X^*$

examples.content: Take $X=c_0$, so $X^*=\ell^1$ and $X^{**}=\ell^\infty$. The standard basis $(e_n)\subseteq\ell^1$ satisfies $e_n\overset{w^*}{\to}0$, because $\langle e_n,x\rangle=x_n\to0$ for every $x\in c_0$. But $e_n\not\rightharpoonup0$ weakly in $\ell^1$: testing against $\mathbf 1=(1,1,\dots)\in\ell^\infty=X^{**}$ gives $\langle e_n,\mathbf 1\rangle=1\not\to0$. This is exactly the failure of $c_0$ to be reflexive.
examples.label: A genuinely coarser example

examples.content: For $\dim X=\infty$, $\sigma(X^*,X)$ is not metrizable on $X^*$ globally. It is metrizable on the norm-bounded set $B_{X^*}$ precisely when $X$ is separable, which is what makes sequential extraction legitimate for separable $X$ and forces the use of nets in general.
examples.label: Not metrizable on all of $X^*$

assumptions: $X$ is a normed vector space; $X^*$ is its continuous dual.
The construction requires a distinguished predual $X$, so it is a topology on a dual space, not on an abstract Banach space.
properties: Locally convex; $(X^*,\sigma(X^*,X))$ is a topological vector space.
Hausdorff, since $\hat X$ separates points of $X^*$: if $x^*\neq y^*$ then $x^*(x)\neq y^*(x)$ for some $x\in X$, directly from the definition of equality of functions. No Hahn-Banach is needed here.
Coarser than $\sigma(X^*,X^{**})$, which is coarser than the dual-norm topology.
Makes $B_{X^*}$ compact (Banach-Alaoglu), which the two finer topologies do not in general.

concepts.label: Weakly bounded set

content.statement: A set is weakly bounded if every continuous linear functional is bounded on it.
content.definition: Weak boundedness means boundedness after testing by every element of the dual space.
content.formal: Let $X$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K$ and $A\subseteq X$. Then $$A\ \text{weakly bounded}\quad:\Longleftrightarrow\quad\forall x^*\in X^*:\ \sup_{a\in A}|x^*(a)|<\infty.$$ The bound is allowed to depend on $x^*$; requiring one bound valid for all $x^*$ simultaneously would be norm boundedness. That the two coincide for $X$ Banach is the content of the uniform boundedness principle.
content.intuition: The set may look large in X, but every scalar probe sees only bounded values.

assumptions: $X$ is a normed space.

content.definition: $$\ell^2 \text{ is the square-summable sequence space with inner product } \langle x,y \rangle = \sum x_n \overline{y_n}.$$
content.formal: $$\ell^2 \text{ with } \langle x,y \rangle = \sum_n x_n \overline{y_n}.$$
content.intuition: The canonical separable infinite-dimensional Hilbert space.

concepts.label: Cauchy-Schwarz inequality

content.statement: The modulus of an inner product is bounded by the product of the norms, with equality exactly for linearly dependent vectors.
content.formal: Let $(H,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)$ be an inner product space over $\mathbb K$. Then $$\forall x,y\in H:\quad|\langle x,y\rangle|\leq\|x\|\,\|y\|,\qquad\|x\|=\sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle},$$ with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.
content.intuition: An inner product cannot exceed what the two lengths allow; the deficit measures the angle between the vectors. It is the inequality that makes $\sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle}$ satisfy the triangle inequality, hence be a norm at all.
content.gloss: Everything is a number here: $\langle x,y\rangle$ is a scalar, $|\langle x,y\rangle|$ and the two norms are non-negative reals. Completeness plays no role.

examples.content: The triangle inequality follows: $\|x+y\|^2=\|x\|^2+2\operatorname{Re}\langle x,y\rangle+\|y\|^2\leq\|x\|^2+2\|x\|\|y\|+\|y\|^2=(\|x\|+\|y\|)^2$. Without Cauchy-Schwarz, $\sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle}$ is not known to be a norm.
examples.label: It is what makes the induced norm a norm

examples.content: For fixed $y$, the map $x\mapsto\langle x,y\rangle$ is a bounded linear functional of norm exactly $\|y\|$, by Cauchy-Schwarz for the upper bound and $x=y$ for attainment. This is the easy half of the Riesz representation theorem.
examples.label: Continuity of the inner product

assumptions: $(H,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)$ is an inner product space; completeness is not required.
Positive definiteness of the inner product is used for the case $y\neq0$ and for the equality condition.

steps.content: If $y=0$ then both sides are $0$. Assume $y\neq0$, so $\langle y,y\rangle>0$ by positive definiteness.

Put $\lambda=\dfrac{\langle x,y\rangle}{\langle y,y\rangle}$ and expand, using linearity in the first slot and conjugate-linearity in the second: $$0\leq\|x-\lambda y\|^2=\langle x,x\rangle-\overline{\lambda}\langle x,y\rangle-\lambda\overline{\langle x,y\rangle}+|\lambda|^2\langle y,y\rangle=\|x\|^2-\frac{|\langle x,y\rangle|^2}{\|y\|^2}.$$

Rearranging gives $|\langle x,y\rangle|^2\leq\|x\|^2\|y\|^2$, and taking square roots gives the inequality. Equality holds exactly when $\|x-\lambda y\|=0$, i.e. $x=\lambda y$, which is linear dependence.

content.statement: The operator is compact and self-adjoint on a Hilbert space.
content.intuition: Compactness gives eigenvalue accumulation control; self-adjointness gives orthogonality.

content.statement: Eigenvalues of a compact self-adjoint operator are real; eigenspaces for distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal; every nonzero eigenspace is finite-dimensional.
content.formal: If $T=T^*$ is compact, then $$Tx=\lambda x\Longrightarrow\lambda\in\mathbb R,$$ $$\lambda_1\ne\lambda_2\Longrightarrow E_{\lambda_1}\perp E_{\lambda_2},$$ and $$\lambda\ne0\Longrightarrow\dim E_\lambda<\infty.$$
content.intuition: Self-adjointness controls the geometry of eigenvectors, while compactness forbids an infinite orthonormal family at any nonzero eigenvalue.

steps.content: From $Tx=\lambda x$ and $T=T^*$, compare $\langle Tx,x\rangle$ with its conjugate to obtain $\lambda=\overline\lambda$.
For eigenvectors $x_1,x_2$, self-adjointness gives $(\lambda_1-\lambda_2)\langle x_1,x_2\rangle=0$.
On $E_\lambda$ with $\lambda\ne0$, the compact operator $T/\lambda$ is the identity. The identity is compact only in finite dimension.

concepts.label: Hilbert projection theorem

content.statement: Every point of a Hilbert space has a unique nearest point in any nonempty closed convex subset.
content.formal: Let $H$ be a Hilbert space, $C\subseteq H$ nonempty, closed and convex, and $x\in H$. Then $$\exists!\,c_0\in C:\quad\|x-c_0\|=\operatorname{dist}(x,C)=\inf_{c\in C}\|x-c\|.$$ When $C=M$ is a closed subspace, the nearest point map $P_M:H\to M$ is linear, satisfies $P_M^2=P_M$, $\|P_M\|\leq1$, and yields the orthogonal decomposition $$H=M\oplus M^\perp,\qquad x=P_Mx+(x-P_Mx),\quad x-P_Mx\in M^\perp.$$
content.intuition: Orthogonal projection is the engine of Hilbert space geometry. The inner product makes the distance function strictly convex through the parallelogram identity, so a minimiser cannot be attained twice, and completeness guarantees the minimising sequence actually converges.
content.gloss: This is the existence result the Riesz representation theorem runs on: it is what produces a nonzero vector orthogonal to a closed proper subspace.

examples.content: Without convexity uniqueness fails: in $H=\mathbb R^2$ take $C=\{(x,y):x^2+y^2=1\}$, the unit circle, which is closed and nonempty but not convex. The point $x=(0,0)$ is at distance $1$ from every point of $C$, so the nearest point is not unique. Existence can also fail in infinite dimensions for closed non-convex sets.
examples.label: Convexity is load-bearing

examples.content: Take $C=\{y\in H:\|y\|<1\}$, the open unit ball, which is convex but not closed, and $x$ with $\|x\|=2$. Then $\operatorname{dist}(x,C)=1$ but no point of $C$ attains it, since the infimum is approached only as $\|y\|\to1$.
examples.label: Closedness is load-bearing

examples.content: In an incomplete inner product space the minimising sequence is Cauchy but need not converge. In $c_{00}$ with the $\ell^2$ inner product, the closed convex set $C=\{y\in c_{00}:\sum_n y_n/n=1\}$ admits a minimising sequence for the distance to $0$ whose limit lies in $\ell^2\setminus c_{00}$, so no minimiser exists in the space.
examples.label: Completeness is load-bearing

examples.content: The result is genuinely Hilbertian, since the parallelogram identity characterises inner product norms. In $(\mathbb R^2,\|\cdot\|_\infty)$ with $C=\{(t,0):t\in[-1,1]\}$ closed and convex, the point $(0,1)$ is at distance $1$ from every point of $C$, so uniqueness fails.
examples.label: Fails in general Banach spaces

assumptions: $H$ is a Hilbert space; completeness is used to converge the minimising sequence.
$C$ is nonempty, closed and convex; each of the three is load-bearing.
The norm comes from an inner product, so the parallelogram identity is available.

steps.content: Let $d=\inf_{c\in C}\|x-c\|$, finite since $C\neq\emptyset$. By definition of infimum choose $(c_n)\subseteq C$ with $\|x-c_n\|\to d$.

Apply the parallelogram identity $\|a+b\|^2+\|a-b\|^2=2\|a\|^2+2\|b\|^2$ to $a=x-c_n$, $b=x-c_m$: $$\|2x-(c_n+c_m)\|^2+\|c_m-c_n\|^2=2\|x-c_n\|^2+2\|x-c_m\|^2.$$ Since $C$ is convex, $\tfrac{1}{2}(c_n+c_m)\in C$, so $\|2x-(c_n+c_m)\|^2=4\|x-\tfrac{1}{2}(c_n+c_m)\|^2\geq4d^2$. Rearranging, $$\|c_m-c_n\|^2\leq2\|x-c_n\|^2+2\|x-c_m\|^2-4d^2\xrightarrow[n,m\to\infty]{}2d^2+2d^2-4d^2=0.$$ Hence $(c_n)$ is Cauchy. Convexity is used exactly here.
Completeness of $H$ gives $c_n\to c_0$ for some $c_0\in H$, and closedness of $C$ gives $c_0\in C$. Continuity of the norm gives $\|x-c_0\|=\lim_n\|x-c_n\|=d$.
If $c_0,c_1\in C$ both attain $d$, the same parallelogram estimate with $c_n=c_0$, $c_m=c_1$ gives $\|c_1-c_0\|^2\leq2d^2+2d^2-4d^2=0$, so $c_0=c_1$.

Let $C=M$ be a closed subspace and $u=x-P_Mx$. For any $m\in M$ and $t\in\mathbb K$ minimality gives $\|u\|^2\leq\|u-tm\|^2=\|u\|^2-2\operatorname{Re}\big(\overline{t}\langle u,m\rangle\big)+|t|^2\|m\|^2$. Choosing $t=s\langle u,m\rangle$ with $s>0$ small forces $|\langle u,m\rangle|^2\leq s\,|\langle u,m\rangle|^2\|m\|^2/2$ in the limit, hence $\langle u,m\rangle=0$. So $u\in M^\perp$ and $H=M\oplus M^\perp$.

content.definition: A complete inner product space.
content.formal: A Hilbert space is a pair $(H,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)$ where $H$ is an inner product space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ that is complete with respect to the induced norm $$\|x\|=\sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle}.$$ Completeness means every Cauchy sequence converges in $H$: $$\forall(x_n)\subseteq H:\ \big(\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists N\ \forall m,n\geq N:\|x_n-x_m\|<\varepsilon\big)\implies\exists x\in H:\ \|x_n-x\|\to0.$$
content.intuition: Euclidean geometry after passing to infinite dimensions.

concepts.label: Hilbert-space adjoint

content.definition: The Hilbert adjoint of a bounded operator between Hilbert spaces is the unique bounded operator moving the operator across the inner product.
content.formal: Let $H,K$ be Hilbert spaces and $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$. There is a unique $T^*\in\mathcal B(K,H)$ with $$\forall x\in H\ \forall y\in K:\quad\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H.$$ Existence: for fixed $y\in K$ the map $x\mapsto\langle Tx,y\rangle_K$ is a bounded linear functional on $H$, so by the Riesz representation theorem there is a unique vector, called $T^*y$, representing it. Properties: $$\|T^*\|=\|T\|,\qquad T^{**}=T,\qquad (\lambda T)^*=\overline{\lambda}\,T^*,\qquad \|T^*T\|=\|T\|^2.$$
content.intuition: The infinite-dimensional conjugate transpose. Where the Banach adjoint reroutes probes, the Hilbert adjoint stays among vectors, because Riesz lets every probe be named by a vector.
content.gloss: Type discipline: this $T^*$ maps $K\to H$, i.e. vectors to vectors, unlike the Banach adjoint $Y^*\to X^*$ which maps functionals to functionals. The map $T\mapsto T^*$ is conjugate-linear, and the conjugation is inherited from the conjugate-linearity of the Riesz map.

examples.content: For $H=K=\mathbb C^n$ with the standard inner product and $T$ given by a matrix $A$, the adjoint is the conjugate transpose $A^*=\overline{A}^{\,\mathsf T}$. Self-adjointness $T=T^*$ is Hermitian symmetry.
examples.label: Matrices

examples.content: $\ker T^*=(\operatorname{ran}T)^\perp$ and $\overline{\operatorname{ran}T}=(\ker T^*)^\perp$. These are the Hilbert-space form of the rank-nullity relations and are the standard tool for deciding solvability of $Tx=y$.
examples.label: Kernel and range relation

examples.content: Existence of $T^*$ is not automatic; it is exactly one application of the Riesz representation theorem per vector $y\in K$. On an incomplete inner product space the adjoint may fail to exist, since the representing vector need not lie in the space.
examples.label: Depends on Riesz representation

assumptions: $H,K$ are Hilbert spaces; completeness is used through the Riesz representation theorem.
$T$ is bounded; unbounded operators have adjoints only under densely-defined domain conditions.

concepts.label: Hilbert-space Riesz Representation Theorem

content.statement: Every continuous linear functional on a Hilbert space is given by the inner product against a unique vector, and the correspondence is isometric.
content.formal: Let $H$ be a Hilbert space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ with inner product linear in the first slot. Then $$\forall f\in H^*\ \exists!\,y\in H\ \forall x\in H:\quad f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle,$$ and moreover $\|f\|_{H^*}=\|y\|_H$. The vector $y$ is quantified before $x$, so one $y$ serves every $x$. The induced map $$R:H^*\to H,\qquad R(f)=y,$$ is a bijective isometry which is linear when $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$ and conjugate-linear when $\mathbb K=\mathbb C$, since $\overline{\lambda}$ appears on pulling a scalar out of the second slot.
content.intuition: A Hilbert space is its own dual. Every continuous scalar probe on $H$ is already realised by a vector of $H$ measuring against it, so no genuinely new objects appear in $H^*$. The proof finds that vector: $f$ kills a closed hyperplane, and the direction orthogonal to that hyperplane, correctly scaled, is the representing vector.
content.gloss: Type check: $f$ is a functional on $H$, $y$ is an element of $H$, $\langle x,y\rangle$ is a scalar. The theorem identifies two different kinds of object via $R$, and it is $R$ that is conjugate-linear, not the inner product.

examples.content: The theorem fails on incomplete inner product spaces, because the projection theorem needs completeness to produce the orthogonal direction. Take $H_0=c_{00}\subseteq\ell^2$, the finitely supported sequences, and $$f(x)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{x_n}{n},$$ a finite sum for each $x\in H_0$, so $f$ is well defined, linear and bounded with $\|f\|=\|(1/n)_n\|_2$. Any representing vector would have to be $y=(1/n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$, which lies in $\ell^2$ but not in $H_0$. So no $y\in H_0$ represents $f$.
examples.label: Completeness is load-bearing

examples.content: For a discontinuous linear functional the kernel is dense rather than closed, so $(\ker f)^\perp=\{0\}$ and step three produces nothing. On any infinite-dimensional Hilbert space a Hamel basis yields an unbounded linear functional, and no vector represents it: $y$ would make $f=\langle\cdot,y\rangle$ bounded by Cauchy-Schwarz.
examples.label: Continuity is load-bearing

examples.content: For $\mathbb K=\mathbb C$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb C$, the functional $\lambda f$ is represented by $\overline{\lambda}y$, since $(\lambda f)(x)=\lambda\langle x,y\rangle=\langle x,\overline{\lambda}y\rangle$. Hence $R(\lambda f)=\overline{\lambda}R(f)$, so $H^*$ is anti-isomorphic, not isomorphic, to $H$ as a complex vector space. With the opposite convention (inner product linear in the second slot) the conjugates move to the other side.
examples.label: The map $R$ is conjugate-linear, not linear

examples.content: Applying the theorem twice gives a linear isometric bijection $H\to H^{**}$ (two conjugations compose to the identity), and this map is the canonical embedding $J$. Hence every Hilbert space is reflexive, and by the reflexivity criterion every bounded sequence in $H$ has a weakly convergent subsequence.
examples.label: Consequence: Hilbert spaces are reflexive

examples.content: Every $f\in(\ell^2)^*$ has the form $f(x)=\sum_n x_n\overline{y_n}$ for a unique $y\in\ell^2$ with $\|f\|=\|y\|_2$. This is the $p=2$ instance of $\ell^p$ duality, and the only one where the dual is the space itself.
examples.label: Concrete case $H=\ell^2$

assumptions: $H$ is a Hilbert space, i.e. an inner product space complete in the induced norm. Completeness is used via the projection theorem and cannot be dropped.
$f$ is a continuous (equivalently bounded) linear functional; continuity is used exactly once, to make $\ker f$ closed.
The inner product is taken linear in the first slot and conjugate-linear in the second; with the other convention the conjugates in the formulas move.
No separability is required.

steps.content: If $f=0$, take $y=0$; then $f(x)=0=\langle x,0\rangle$ for all $x$. Assume from now on $f\neq0$.

steps.role: the kernel is a closed proper subspace
steps.content: Since $f$ is linear, $\ker f$ is a subspace; since $f$ is continuous, $\ker f=f^{-1}(\{0\})$ is closed as the preimage of the closed set $\{0\}$. Since $f\neq0$, it is proper. Continuity is used exactly here, and this is the only place it is needed.

Because $\ker f$ is a closed proper subspace of the Hilbert space $H$, the projection theorem gives the orthogonal decomposition $H=\ker f\oplus(\ker f)^\perp$ with $(\ker f)^\perp
eq\{0\}$. Choose $z\in(\ker f)^\perp$ with $z
eq0$; then $f(z)
eq0$, since $z\in\ker f$ would force $z\in\ker f\cap(\ker f)^\perp=\{0\}$.

Define explicitly $$y=\frac{\overline{f(z)}}{\|z\|^2}\,z\ \in H.$$ This is the one construction the proof performs; the conjugate is required so that $y$ sits in the second, conjugate-linear slot of the inner product. Check it works on $z$: $$\langle z,y\rangle=\Big\langle z,\tfrac{\overline{f(z)}}{\|z\|^2}z\Big\rangle=\frac{f(z)}{\|z\|^2}\langle z,z\rangle=f(z),$$ using conjugate-linearity in the second slot, which conjugates $\overline{f(z)}$ back to $f(z)$.

Let $x\in H$ be arbitrary and set $$u=x-\frac{f(x)}{f(z)}z,$$ which is legitimate since $f(z)\neq0$. Then by linearity $f(u)=f(x)-\frac{f(x)}{f(z)}f(z)=0$, so $u\in\ker f$, hence $\langle u,y\rangle=0$ because $y$ is a scalar multiple of $z\in(\ker f)^\perp$. Therefore $$\langle x,y\rangle=\Big\langle u+\tfrac{f(x)}{f(z)}z,\ y\Big\rangle=0+\frac{f(x)}{f(z)}\langle z,y\rangle=\frac{f(x)}{f(z)}f(z)=f(x).$$

Two inequalities. By Cauchy-Schwarz, $|f(x)|=|\langle x,y\rangle|\leq\|x\|\,\|y\|$, so $\|f\|\leq\|y\|$. Conversely, if $y\neq0$, evaluating at the unit vector $x=y/\|y\|$ gives $$|f(y/\|y\|)|=\frac{|\langle y,y\rangle|}{\|y\|}=\frac{\|y\|^2}{\|y\|}=\|y\|,$$ so $\|f\|\geq\|y\|$. Hence $\|f\|=\|y\|$; the case $y=0$ is immediate.

Suppose $\langle x,y_1\rangle=f(x)=\langle x,y_2\rangle$ for all $x\in H$. Then $\langle x,y_1-y_2\rangle=0$ for all $x$; taking $x=y_1-y_2$ gives $\|y_1-y_2\|^2=0$, so $y_1=y_2$ by positive definiteness of the inner product.

content.definition: A vector space equipped with an inner product inducing a norm.
content.formal: An inner product space is a pair $(H,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)$ with $H$ a vector space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:H\times H\to\mathbb K$ satisfying, for all $x,y,z\in H$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb K$: $$\begin{aligned}&\text{(i) linearity in the first slot:} && \langle x+\lambda y,z\rangle=\langle x,z\rangle+\lambda\langle y,z\rangle,\\ &\text{(ii) conjugate symmetry:} && \langle x,y\rangle=\overline{\langle y,x\rangle},\\ &\text{(iii) positive definiteness:} && \langle x,x\rangle\geq0\ \text{ and }\ \langle x,x\rangle=0\iff x=0.\end{aligned}$$ Conditions (i) and (ii) together give conjugate linearity in the second slot, so the form is sesquilinear over $\mathbb C$ and bilinear over $\mathbb R$.
content.intuition: A vector space where angles and orthogonality make sense.

concepts.label: Lax-Milgram Theorem

content.statement: A bounded coercive sesquilinear form on a Hilbert space represents every bounded functional uniquely, generalising Riesz representation to non-symmetric forms.
content.formal: Let $H$ be a Hilbert space and $a:H\times H\to\mathbb K$ sesquilinear with $$\exists C>0\ \forall u,v\in H:\ |a(u,v)|\leq C\|u\|\|v\|\qquad\text{(boundedness)},$$ $$\exists\alpha>0\ \forall u\in H:\ |a(u,u)|\geq\alpha\|u\|^2\qquad\text{(coercivity)}.$$ Then $$\forall f\in H^*\ \exists!\,u\in H\ \forall v\in H:\quad a(u,v)=f(v),$$ and $\|u\|\leq\alpha^{-1}\|f\|$. Taking $a(u,v)=\langle v,u\rangle$ recovers the Riesz representation theorem with $C=\alpha=1$.
content.intuition: Riesz representation says the inner product represents every functional. Lax-Milgram says any form comparable to the inner product from above and below does the same, even without symmetry. Coercivity is what replaces positive definiteness, and it is the hypothesis that makes the associated operator invertible.
content.gloss: The route: $a$ induces $A\in\mathcal B(H)$ by $a(u,v)=\langle Au,v\rangle$ via Riesz; boundedness makes $A$ bounded, coercivity makes $A$ bounded below and surjective, so $u=A^{-1}(Rf)$.

examples.content: Without a lower bound the associated operator need not be invertible. On $H=\ell^2$ take $a(u,v)=\sum_n n^{-1}u_n\overline{v_n}$, which is bounded and satisfies $a(u,u)>0$ for $u\neq0$ but is not coercive. The functional $f(v)=\sum_n n^{-1/2}\overline{v_n}$ is bounded, yet the equation $a(u,v)=f(v)$ forces $u_n=n^{1/2}$, which is not in $\ell^2$. Strict positivity is not enough; a uniform $\alpha$ is required.
examples.label: Coercivity is load-bearing

examples.content: If $a$ is additionally symmetric it is an equivalent inner product on $H$ and the result is Riesz representation in that inner product. The content of Lax-Milgram is precisely the non-symmetric case, which is why it handles convection-diffusion problems where the symmetric theory does not apply.
examples.label: Symmetry is not required

examples.content: For $-\Delta u=f$ on a bounded domain with Dirichlet conditions, take $H=H_0^1(\Omega)$ and $a(u,v)=\int_\Omega\nabla u\cdot\overline{\nabla v}$. The Poincare inequality supplies coercivity, so Lax-Milgram gives a unique weak solution. This is the standard existence argument in the variational theory of elliptic equations.
examples.label: Weak formulation of elliptic PDE

assumptions: $H$ is a Hilbert space; completeness is essential, entering through Riesz representation.
$a$ is sesquilinear, bounded, and coercive; coercivity cannot be weakened to strict positivity.
Symmetry of $a$ is not assumed.

content.statement: Spectral theorems reduce suitable operator questions to scalar spectral data.
content.intuition: Diagonalize the operator conceptually, then analyze eigenvalues/spectrum.

concepts.label: Orthogonal complement

content.definition: The orthogonal complement of a subset of an inner product space is the set of vectors orthogonal to every element of it.
content.formal: Let $H$ be an inner product space and $S\subseteq H$ any subset. Then $$S^\perp=\{y\in H:\langle x,y\rangle=0\ \text{for all }x\in S\}.$$ Note $S$ need not be a subspace, but $S^\perp$ always is, and is always closed: $$S^\perp=\bigcap_{x\in S}\ker\langle x,\cdot\rangle$$ is an intersection of kernels of continuous functionals. If $H$ is Hilbert and $M\subseteq H$ is a closed subspace, then $$H=M\oplus M^\perp\qquad\text{and}\qquad (M^\perp)^\perp=M.$$ For general $S$, $(S^\perp)^\perp=\overline{\operatorname{span}}\,S$.
content.intuition: Everything the vectors of $S$ cannot see. Taking the complement twice recovers not $S$ itself but the closed subspace it generates, so $\perp\perp$ is a closure operation.
content.gloss: Closedness of $S^\perp$ is automatic and free; the decomposition $H=M\oplus M^\perp$ is not, and needs completeness plus closedness of $M$.

examples.content: Take $H=\ell^2$ and $M=c_{00}$, a dense non-closed subspace. Then $M^\perp=\{0\}$, so $M\oplus M^\perp=M\neq H$. Density makes the complement collapse, and $(M^\perp)^\perp=\overline{M}=\ell^2\neq M$.
examples.label: $M$ must be closed for the decomposition

examples.content: For a subspace $M$ of a Hilbert space, $M$ is dense if and only if $M^\perp=\{0\}$. This is the standard route to proving a family is total, e.g. showing polynomials are dense in $L^2[0,1]$ by showing only $0$ is orthogonal to all of them.
examples.label: Density criterion

assumptions: $H$ is an inner product space; $S^\perp$ is defined and closed without completeness.
The decomposition $H=M\oplus M^\perp$ requires $H$ complete and $M$ closed.

content.definition: A maximal orthonormal set whose closed linear span is the Hilbert space.
content.intuition: Coordinate axes for Hilbert space.

content.definition: A linear operator P satisfying P^2=P.
content.intuition: A map that keeps one component and kills another.

content.definition: An operator on a Hilbert space equal to its Hilbert-space adjoint.
content.formal: $T=T^\ast$, equivalently $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,Ty\rangle$.
content.intuition: Infinite-dimensional analogue of a Hermitian matrix.

content.statement: A compact self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space admits an orthonormal eigenbasis for the closure of its range and a spectral decomposition.
content.formal: If $T$ is compact self-adjoint on $H$, then nonzero spectrum consists of real eigenvalues with finite-dimensional eigenspaces accumulating only at 0, and $H$ decomposes orthogonally into eigenspaces plus $\ker(T)$.
content.intuition: Compact self-adjoint operators behave like diagonal Hermitian matrices.

content.definition: The set of scalars lambda for which T-lambda I is not invertible in the appropriate operator algebra.
content.formal: sigma(T)={lambda: T-lambda I is not bijective with bounded inverse}.
content.intuition: The infinite-dimensional replacement for eigenvalues.

concepts.label: Hahn-Banach extension theorem

content.statement: A real linear functional dominated by a sublinear functional on a subspace extends to the whole vector space while remaining dominated by the same sublinear functional.
content.formal: Let $E$ be a real vector space and let $p:E\to\mathbb R$ be sublinear. If $V$ is a subspace of $E$ and if $f:V\to\mathbb R$ is a linear functional such that $f(x)\leq p(x)$ for every $x\in V$, then there exists an extension $\widehat f:E\to\mathbb R$ of $f$ that is linear and satisfies $\widehat f(x)\leq p(x)$ for every $x\in E$.
content.formula: $$\begin{aligned} &E\text{ real vector space},\quad V\leq E,\quad p:E\to\mathbb R\text{ sublinear},\\ &f:V\to\mathbb R\text{ linear},\quad f(x)\leq p(x)\quad(x\in V),\\ &\Longrightarrow \exists\widehat f:E\to\mathbb R\text{ linear}:\quad \widehat f|_V=f\quad\text{and}\quad \widehat f(x)\leq p(x)\quad(x\in E). \end{aligned}$$
content.intuition: The functional $f$ is a linear height function defined only on the slice $V$. The sublinear functional $p$ is a one-sided ceiling over all of $E$. Hahn-Banach says that the height function can be extended to the whole space without crossing that ceiling.

examples.content: If $p$ is a norm or a norm multiple, then domination by $p$ becomes a norm estimate. This is how the norm-preserving Hahn-Banach theorem for normed spaces follows from the extension theorem.
examples.label: Norm control from sublinear domination

examples.content: The theorem guarantees existence, not uniqueness. Hahn-Banach extensions are generally non-constructive.
examples.label: Non-uniqueness

assumptions: $E$ is a real vector space.
$V\leq E$ is a linear subspace.
$p:E\to\mathbb R$ is sublinear.
$f:V\to\mathbb R$ is linear.
$f(x)\leq p(x)$ for every $x\in V$.

steps.content: Construct a sublinear functional $q$ on $E$ such that $q|_V=f$ and $q\leq p$.
Use the order on sublinear functionals to choose a minimal sublinear functional $q_0$ on $E$ satisfying $q_0\leq q$.
The minimality of $q_0$ implies that $q_0$ is linear.
Set $\widehat f=q_0$. Then $\widehat f$ is linear and $\widehat f\leq p$ on $E$.
Since $\widehat f\leq q$ and $q|_V=f$, one gets $\widehat f\leq f$ on $V$. Applying the same inequality to $-x$ gives $\widehat f(x)\geq f(x)$ for $x\in V$. Hence $\widehat f|_V=f$.

concepts.label: Hahn-Banach theorem for complex normed spaces

content.statement: A bounded complex-linear functional on a subspace of a complex normed space extends to the whole space with the same norm.
content.formal: Suppose $X$ is a complex normed vector space and let $V$ be a complex linear subspace of $X$. If $f\in V^*$, then there exists an extension $\widehat f\in X^*$ such that $\widehat f|_V=f$ and $\|\widehat f\|=\|f\|$.
content.formula: $$X\text{ complex normed},\quad V\leq X,\quad f\in V^*\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \exists\widehat f\in X^*: \widehat f|_V=f,\ \|\widehat f\| = \|f\|.$$
content.intuition: The complex theorem is reduced to the real theorem. First extend the real part of $f$. Then recover the full complex-linear functional using multiplication by $i$.
notation: $\widehat f(x)=\widehat f_0(x)-i\widehat f_0(ix)$: reconstructed complex-linear extension

examples.content: For $x_0\neq0$, set $V=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}\{x_0\}$ and define $f(\alpha x_0)=\alpha\|x_0\|$. Hahn-Banach gives $\widehat f\in X^*$ with $\|\widehat f\|=1$ and $\widehat f(x_0)=\|x_0\|$.
examples.label: Complex norming functional

examples.content: The real theorem is not applied directly to the complex-valued map $f$. It is applied to $f_0=\operatorname{Re}f$, and the complex-linear extension is reconstructed afterward.
examples.label: Reduction to the real case

assumptions: $X$ is a complex normed vector space.
$V\leq X$ is a complex linear subspace.
$f\in V^*$ is bounded and complex-linear.

steps.content: Define $f_0:V\to\mathbb R$ by $f_0(x)=\operatorname{Re}f(x)$, and regard $X$ and $V$ as real normed spaces.
By the real Hahn-Banach theorem, extend $f_0$ to a real-linear functional $\widehat f_0:X\to\mathbb R$ with the same norm.
Define $\widehat f:X\to\mathbb C$ by $\widehat f(x)=\widehat f_0(x)-i\widehat f_0(ix)$.

For $x\in V$, complex-linearity of $f$ gives $f_0(ix)=-\operatorname{Im}f(x)$, so $\widehat f(x)=f(x)$. Also $\widehat f(ix)=i\widehat f(x)$; together with real-linearity, this gives complex-linearity.
The construction gives $\|\widehat f\|\leq\|f\|$. Since $\widehat f$ extends $f$, also $\|\widehat f\|\geq\|f\|$. Therefore $\|\widehat f\|=\|f\|$.

concepts.label: Hahn-Banach theorem for real normed spaces

content.statement: A bounded real-linear functional on a subspace of a real normed space extends to the whole space with the same norm.
content.formal: Suppose $X$ is a real normed vector space and let $V$ be a linear subspace of $X$. If $f\in V^*$, then there exists an extension $\widehat f\in X^*$ such that $\widehat f|_V=f$ and $\|\widehat f\|=\|f\|$.
content.formula: $$X\text{ real normed},\quad V\leq X,\quad f\in V^*\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \exists\widehat f\in X^*: \widehat f|_V=f,\ \|\widehat f\|=\|f\|.$$
content.intuition: The functional $f$ measures vectors on the slice $V$. Hahn-Banach extends this measurement to all of $X$ without increasing its maximal slope. The proof uses the ceiling $p(x)=\|f\|\|x\|$.

examples.content: For $x_0\neq0$, set $V=\operatorname{span}\{x_0\}$ and define $f(\alpha x_0)=\alpha\|x_0\|$. Then $\|f\|=1$. Hahn-Banach gives $\widehat f\in X^*$ with $\|\widehat f\|=1$ and $\widehat f(x_0)=\|x_0\|$.
examples.label: Norming functional

examples.content: The extension need not be unique. Hahn-Banach gives existence of a norm-preserving extension, not a canonical formula.
examples.label: Non-uniqueness

assumptions: $X$ is a real normed vector space.
$V\leq X$ is a linear subspace.
$f\in V^*$ is bounded and real-linear.

steps.content: Define $p:X\to\mathbb R$ by $p(x)=\|f\|\|x\|$. This is sublinear.
For $x\in V$, $f(x)\leq |f(x)|\leq\|f\|\|x\|=p(x)$. Hence $f\leq p$ on $V$.
By the Hahn-Banach extension theorem, there exists a linear extension $\widehat f:X\to\mathbb R$ such that $\widehat f|_V=f$ and $\widehat f\leq p$ on $X$.
The domination estimate gives $\|\widehat f\|\leq\|f\|$. Since $\widehat f$ extends $f$, also $\|\widehat f\|\geq\|f\|$. Hence $\|\widehat f\|=\|f\|$.

concepts.label: Norm as a sublinear functional

content.statement: Every norm is a sublinear functional.
content.definition: The norm on a normed vector space is positively homogeneous and subadditive.
content.intuition: The norm is the basic domination function in Hahn-Banach.

assumptions: $X$ is a normed vector space.

content.statement: Positive homogeneity means that scaling an input by a nonnegative scalar scales the output by the same scalar.
content.formal: A function $p:E\to\mathbb R$ on a real vector space is positively homogeneous if $p(\alpha x)=\alpha p(x)$ for every $x\in E$ and every scalar $\alpha\geq 0$.
content.intuition: Positive homogeneity says the function measures size linearly along each ray starting at the origin. If you move twice as far in the same direction, the value doubles.

examples.content: For a norm, $\|\alpha x\|=|\alpha|\|x\|$. In particular, for $\alpha\geq0$, $\|\alpha x\|=\alpha\|x\|$, so every norm is positively homogeneous.

concepts.label: Separation of closed convex sets

content.statement: A point outside a closed convex set in a locally convex space can be strictly separated from the set by a continuous linear functional; for a balanced set containing zero, separation can be expressed using absolute values.
content.formal: If $C\subset X$ is closed and convex and $x_0\notin C$, then some $f\in X^*$ satisfies $$\sup_{x\in C}\operatorname{Re}f(x)<\operatorname{Re}f(x_0).$$ If $C$ is also balanced and $0\in C$, one may arrange $$\sup_{x\in C}|f(x)|<|f(x_0)|.$$
content.intuition: Local convexity supplies a continuous gauge, and Hahn-Banach converts that gauge into a scalar witness separating the point from the set.

assumptions: $X$ is a complex locally convex topological vector space.
$C$ is closed and convex.
$x_0\notin C$.

content.statement: Hahn-Banach gives, for x != 0, a continuous functional x* with x*(x) != 0.
content.intuition: Dual functionals can detect nonzero vectors.

content.definition: A positively homogeneous and subadditive real-valued map on a real vector space.
content.formal: $p(\alpha x)=\alpha p(x)$ for $\alpha\geq 0$ and $p(x+y)\leq p(x)+p(y)$.
content.intuition: A one-sided convex bound for a linear functional.

concepts.label: Zorn's lemma

content.statement: If every chain in a partially ordered set has an upper bound, then the poset has a maximal element.
content.formal: Let $(P,\leq)$ be a partially ordered set. Call $C\subseteq P$ a chain if $\leq$ restricted to $C$ is total, i.e. $\forall a,b\in C:\ a\leq b\ \text{or}\ b\leq a$. Then $$\Big(P\neq\emptyset\ \wedge\ \forall\ \text{chains}\ C\subseteq P\ \exists u\in P\ \forall a\in C:\ a\leq u\Big)\implies\exists m\in P\ \forall a\in P:\ \big(m\leq a\implies a=m\big).$$ The element $m$ is maximal, not maximum: it is not required that $a\leq m$ for all $a\in P$. The upper bound $u$ must lie in $P$ but need not lie in $C$.
content.intuition: The maximal-extension engine behind Hahn-Banach. One partially orders the set of partial extensions of a functional, checks that a chain of extensions can be glued into a common extension serving as an upper bound, and Zorn's lemma then supplies a maximal extension, which a separate argument shows must be defined on all of $X$.
content.gloss: Equivalent to the axiom of choice and to the well-ordering theorem, over ZF.

examples.content: The empty poset satisfies the chain condition vacuously (its only chain is $\emptyset$, which has no upper bound requirement met only if some $u\in P$ exists) yet has no maximal element. The hypothesis $P\neq\emptyset$, or equivalently insisting that the empty chain have an upper bound, rules this out.
examples.label: Nonemptiness is load-bearing

examples.content: In the poset of proper subsets of $\{1,2\}$ ordered by inclusion, both $\{1\}$ and $\{2\}$ are maximal, and neither is a maximum. Zorn's lemma asserts existence of a maximal element only, and gives no uniqueness.
examples.label: Maximal is not maximum

examples.content: Take $P=\mathbb N$ with its usual order. The chain $C=P$ has no upper bound in $P$, the hypothesis fails, and indeed $\mathbb N$ has no maximal element. This is the shape of the check one must perform in any application.
examples.label: A chain with no upper bound

assumptions: $(P,\leq)$ is a nonempty partially ordered set.
Every chain in $P$, including the empty chain, has an upper bound lying in $P$.
Zorn's lemma is equivalent to the axiom of choice over ZF; it is an assumption, not a theorem of ZF.

content.statement: A complete metric space is not a countable union of nowhere dense closed sets.
content.formal: If X is complete metric and X=union F_n with F_n closed, then some F_n has nonempty interior.
content.intuition: Completeness prevents a space from being too thin.

steps.content: Assume a complete metric space $X$ is a countable union of closed sets $F_n$ with empty interior.
Recursively construct closed balls $\overline B_n$ with radii tending to zero such that $\overline B_n\subseteq \overline B_{n-1}$ and $\overline B_n\cap F_n=\varnothing$.
The centers of the nested balls form a Cauchy sequence.
Completeness gives a limit point $x\in X$, and the nesting forces $x\in\overline B_n$ for every $n$.
Since $\overline B_n\cap F_n=\varnothing$ for every $n$, the point $x$ lies in none of the $F_n$, contradicting $X=\bigcup_nF_n$.

concepts.label: Bounded Inverse Theorem

content.statement: A bijective bounded linear operator between Banach spaces has bounded inverse.
content.formal: Let $X,Y$ be Banach spaces over $\mathbb K$ and let $T\in\mathcal B(X,Y)$ be a bijection. Then $T^{-1}\in\mathcal B(Y,X)$, that is, $$\exists C\in(0,\infty)\ \forall y\in Y:\quad\|T^{-1}y\|_X\leq C\|y\|_Y.$$ Equivalently, in terms of $T$ itself, there is $c>0$ with $\|Tx\|_Y\geq c\|x\|_X$ for all $x\in X$, so $T$ is bounded below and is a topological isomorphism.
content.intuition: Banach-space bijections are automatically topological isomorphisms. Continuity of the inverse, which in general has to be assumed, comes for free from completeness of both spaces via the open mapping theorem.
content.gloss: A corollary of the open mapping theorem, hence ultimately of Baire category; the completeness of both $X$ and $Y$ is what is really doing the work.

examples.content: Let $X=(c_{00},\|\cdot\|_\infty)$, the finitely supported sequences, which is not complete, and define $T:X\to X$ by $(Tx)_n=x_n/n$. Then $T$ is linear, bounded with $\|T\|=1$, and bijective onto $c_{00}$, but $T^{-1}$ given by $(T^{-1}y)_n=ny_n$ is unbounded, since $T^{-1}e_n=ne_n$. The conclusion fails precisely because $X$ is not Banach.
examples.label: Completeness cannot be dropped

examples.content: For $T\in\mathcal B(X,Y)$ between Banach spaces, $T$ is invertible with bounded inverse if and only if $T$ is surjective and bounded below, i.e. $\exists c>0\ \forall x:\ \|Tx\|\geq c\|x\|$. Bounded below alone gives injectivity and closed range, but not surjectivity.
examples.label: Equivalent formulation: bounded below

examples.content: If a vector space is complete under two norms $\|\cdot\|_1$ and $\|\cdot\|_2$ and one dominates the other, say $\|x\|_2\leq C\|x\|_1$, then applying the theorem to the identity map shows the norms are equivalent. Comparability plus completeness forces equivalence.
examples.label: Comparison of norms

assumptions: $X$ and $Y$ are Banach spaces; completeness of both is required and neither can be dropped.
$T$ is linear, bounded, and bijective.
The result is a corollary of the open mapping theorem, which rests on the Baire category theorem.

steps.content: Let $T:X\to Y$ be bijective, bounded, and linear between Banach spaces. By the open mapping theorem, $T$ maps open sets in $X$ to open sets in $Y$.
A bijection has continuous inverse iff it maps open sets to open sets. Hence $T^{-1}:Y\to X$ is continuous.
For linear maps between normed spaces, continuity is equivalent to boundedness. Thus $T^{-1}$ is bounded.

content.statement: If $S:Y\to Z$ is bounded and injective and $S\circ T:X\to Z$ is bounded, then a linear map $T:X\to Y$ between Banach spaces is bounded.
content.formal: $$S\text{ bounded and injective},\quad S\circ T\text{ bounded}\Longrightarrow T\text{ bounded}.$$
content.intuition: Injectivity lets convergence after applying $S$ identify the only possible graph limit of $T$.

steps.content: If $x_n\to x$ and $Tx_n\to y$, continuity gives $S(Tx_n)\to S(Tx)$ from boundedness of $S\circ T$ and $S(Tx_n)\to S(y)$ from boundedness of $S$.
Uniqueness of limits gives $S(y)=S(Tx)$, and injectivity gives $y=Tx$. The closed graph theorem now implies that $T$ is bounded.

content.definition: The graph ${(x,Tx)}$ is closed in $X \times Y$.
content.intuition: If $x_n \to x$ and $Tx_n \to y$, then $y=Tx$.

content.statement: A linear operator between Banach spaces is bounded if its graph is closed.
content.formal: If $X,Y$ are Banach and $T:X \to Y$ is linear with graph(T) closed in $X \times Y$, then $T$ is bounded. $$\exists C<\infty \text{ such that } ||Tx|| \leq C||x|| \text{ for all } x \in X.$$
content.intuition: A graph-compatible limit rule forces norm continuity.

steps.content: Define $$\|x\|_G=\|x\|_X+\|Tx\|_Y.$$ If the graph of $T$ is closed and $X,Y$ are Banach, then $(X,\|\cdot\|_G)$ is Banach.
The identity map $I:(X,\|\cdot\|_G)\to(X,\|\cdot\|_X)$ is bounded and bijective.
By the bounded inverse theorem, the inverse identity map $I^{-1}:(X,\|\cdot\|_X)\to(X,\|\cdot\|_G)$ is bounded.
Thus there is $C>0$ such that $$\|x\|_X+\|Tx\|_Y\leq C\|x\|_X.$$ Hence $\|Tx\|_Y\leq C\|x\|_X$, so $T$ is bounded.

content.statement: The codomain space is complete in its norm.
content.intuition: Closed graph/open mapping statements need Banach codomain.

content.statement: The domain space is complete in its norm.
content.intuition: Completeness of the domain is crucial for the Baire category argument to work in the proofs of the mapping theorems.

content.statement: A surjective bounded linear operator between Banach spaces maps open sets to open sets.
content.formal: If $T:X \to Y$ is bounded linear and onto, with $X,Y$ Banach, then $T$ is open. $$\forall U \subset X \text{ open}, T(U) \subset Y \text{ is open}.$$
content.intuition: A complete linear surjection cannot crush all neighborhoods.

steps.content: Let $T:X\to Y$ be surjective, bounded, and linear between Banach spaces. Since $X=\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty nB_X$, surjectivity gives $$Y=\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty T(nB_X).$$
Taking closures, Baire's theorem implies that some $\overline{T(nB_X)}$ has nonempty interior.
By linearity and symmetry, there exists $r>0$ such that $$B_Y(0,r)\subseteq\overline{T(B_X)}.$$
A standard iterative approximation argument improves this to $$B_Y(0,r/2)\subseteq T(B_X).$$
Since $T$ sends a neighborhood of $0$ onto a neighborhood of $0$, linearity implies that $T$ maps every open set in $X$ to an open set in $Y$.

content.statement: The graph of T is closed in X x Y.
content.intuition: Sequential limit compatibility replaces an a priori boundedness estimate.

content.statement: For each x, the set {||T_i x||} is bounded.
content.intuition: Each vector is controlled separately before uniform boundedness upgrades the control.

concepts.label: Pointwise limits of bounded linear functionals

content.statement: On a Banach space, a pointwise limit of bounded linear functionals is again a bounded linear functional, and its norm is bounded by the limit inferior of the norms.
content.formal: Let $X$ be a Banach space and let $(f_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence in $X^*$. If $f_n(x)\to f(x)$ for every $x\in X$, then $f\in X^*$ and $\|f\|\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\|f_n\|$.
content.formula: $$\begin{aligned} &X\text{ Banach},\quad (f_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subseteq X^*,\\ &\forall x\in X:\ f_n(x)\to f(x),\\ &\Longrightarrow f\in X^*\ \text{and}\ \|f\|\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\|f_n\|. \end{aligned}$$
content.intuition: Two ingredients with different requirements. Linearity passes through pointwise limits for free — no completeness, no boundedness needed. Boundedness is the real content: pointwise convergence gives $\sup_n|f_n(x)|<\infty$ at each $x$, and completeness of $X$ upgrades this to a *uniform* bound $\sup_n\|f_n\|<\infty$ via the uniform boundedness principle. The norm estimate is then lower semicontinuity of the norm under pointwise limits.

examples.content: Completeness enters only at the uniform-bound step. If $X$ is merely normed, UBP can fail and the pointwise limit may be unbounded. Standard counterexample: $X=c_{00}$ (finitely supported sequences) with the $\ell^\infty$ norm, $f_n(x)=\sum_{k=1}^n x_k$. Each $f_n\in X^*$ with $\|f_n\|=n$; for any fixed $x\in c_{00}$ the sum is eventually constant, so $f_n(x)\to\sum_k x_k=:f(x)$ pointwise, but $f$ is unbounded on the $\ell^\infty$ unit ball.
examples.label: Failure mode without completeness

assumptions: $X$ is a Banach space.
$(f_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ is a sequence of bounded linear functionals on $X$.
$f_n(x)$ converges for every fixed $x\in X$.

steps.content: For $x,y\in X$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, $f(\alpha x+\beta y)=\lim_n f_n(\alpha x+\beta y)=\lim_n\bigl(\alpha f_n(x)+\beta f_n(y)\bigr)=\alpha f(x)+\beta f(y)$. So $f$ is linear.
Fix $x\in X$. Since $(f_n(x))_n$ converges it is bounded, hence $\sup_n|f_n(x)|<\infty$. This holds for every $x$.
The pointwise bounds and completeness of $X$ give, via the uniform boundedness principle, $M:=\sup_n\|f_n\|<\infty$.
For every $x$, $|f(x)|=\lim_n|f_n(x)|\le M\|x\|$. Hence $f$ is bounded, i.e. $f\in X^*$.
Taking $\liminf_n$ in $|f_n(x)|\le\|f_n\|\,\|x\|$ gives $|f(x)|\le(\liminf_n\|f_n\|)\|x\|$ for all $x$, so $\|f\|\le\liminf_n\|f_n\|$.

content.statement: Uniform boundedness shows pointwise limits of bounded linear operators on Banach domains are bounded under pointwise convergence.
content.intuition: A limit operator inherits boundedness from pointwise convergence plus completeness.

content.statement: The linear operator maps X onto Y.
content.intuition: Open mapping requires every target vector to have a preimage.

concepts.label: Uniform Boundedness Principle

content.statement: A pointwise bounded family of bounded linear operators on a Banach space is uniformly bounded.
content.definition: The uniform boundedness principle, also known as the Banach-Steinhaus theorem, states that if a family of bounded linear operators on a Banach space is pointwise bounded, then the operator norms are uniformly bounded.
content.formal: Let $X$ be a Banach space, let $Y$ be a normed space, and let $\{T_i:X\to Y:i\in I\}$ be a family of bounded linear operators. If for every $x\in X$ one has $$\sup_{i\in I}\|T_i x\|<\infty,$$ then $$\sup_{i\in I}\|T_i\|<\infty.$$
content.intuition: Pointwise control looks weak because each vector may have its own bound. Completeness upgrades these separate bounds into one uniform operator-norm bound.

examples.content: Completeness is necessary. On $c_{00}$ with the $\ell^\infty$ norm, define $T_n(x)=\sum_{k=1}^n x_k$. For each fixed $x\in c_{00}$, the sequence $(T_nx)$ is eventually constant, hence bounded. But $\|T_n\|=n$, so the family is not uniformly bounded.

assumptions: $X$ is Banach.
$Y$ is normed.
$T_i:X\to Y$ is bounded and linear for every $i\in I$.
$\sup_i\|T_i x\|<\infty$ for every fixed $x\in X$.

steps.content: For each $n\in\mathbb N$, define $$E_n=\{x\in X:\sup_{i\in I}\|T_i x\|\leq n\}.$$ Each $E_n$ is closed because each $T_i$ is continuous.
The pointwise boundedness assumption gives $$X=\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty E_n.$$
Since $X$ is Banach, it is a complete metric space. By the Baire category theorem, some $E_N$ has nonempty interior.
Thus there exist $x_0\in X$ and $r>0$ such that $B(x_0,r)\subseteq E_N$. For $\|h\|<r$, both $x_0+h$ and $x_0$ are controlled, so $$\sup_i\|T_i h\|\leq 2N.$$
For arbitrary $x\neq0$, apply the previous estimate to $h=(r/2)x/\|x\|$. This gives $$\sup_i\|T_i x\|\leq \frac{4N}{r}\|x\|.$$ Hence $\sup_i\|T_i\|\leq 4N/r<\infty$.

content.statement: A chain is a subset of a partially ordered set in which every two elements are comparable.
content.formal: Let $(P,\leq)$ be a partially ordered set. A subset $\mathcal C\subseteq P$ is called a chain if for every $a,b\in\mathcal C$, either $a\leq b$ or $b\leq a$.
content.intuition: A chain is a single consistent line of growth inside a partially ordered set. In Hahn-Banach, a chain is a family of extensions where each extension is compatible with the others because one extends the other.

examples.content: In $(\mathcal P(E),\subseteq)$, the family $A_1\subseteq A_2\subseteq A_3\subseteq\cdots$ is a chain.

content.statement: A maximal element is an element that cannot be strictly enlarged within the partially ordered set.
content.formal: Let $(P,\leq)$ be a partially ordered set. An element $m\in P$ is maximal if whenever $m\leq p$ for some $p\in P$, one has $p=m$.
content.intuition: Maximal means there is no legal move upward from this object. In Hahn-Banach, a maximal extension is an extension that cannot be extended further while preserving the domination condition.

examples.content: In a family of admissible Hahn-Banach extensions, a maximal element is a pair $(M,h)$ such that no strictly larger admissible pair $(M',h')$ extends it.

content.statement: A partial order is a relation that is reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive.
content.definition: A partial order on a set $P$ is a relation that behaves like an abstract version of $\leq$, except that not every two elements must be comparable.
content.formal: Let $P$ be a set. A relation $\preceq\subseteq P\times P$ is a partial order if, for all $a,b,c\in P$: (i) $a\preceq a$; (ii) if $a\preceq b$ and $b\preceq a$, then $a=b$; and (iii) if $a\preceq b$ and $b\preceq c$, then $a\preceq c$.
content.intuition: A partial order compares objects only when the comparison makes sense. Unlike a total order, it permits incomparable elements.

examples.content: For any set $S$, subset inclusion $A\subseteq B$ defines a partial order on $\mathcal P(S)$.
Divisibility defines a partial order on $\mathbb N$: $a\preceq b$ iff $a$ divides $b$.
Pointwise order defines a partial order on real-valued functions: $f\preceq g$ iff $f(x)\leq g(x)$ for every $x$.

content.statement: A partially ordered set is a set equipped with a reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive binary relation.
content.definition: A partially ordered set, or poset, is an ordered pair $(P,\leq)$, where $P$ is a set and $\leq\,\subseteq P\times P$ is a binary relation satisfying reflexivity, antisymmetry, and transitivity.
content.formal: Let $P$ be a set and let $\leq\,\subseteq P\times P$. Then $(P,\leq)$ is a partially ordered set if and only if $(\forall x\in P)(x\leq x)$, $(\forall x,y\in P)(((x\leq y)\land(y\leq x))\Rightarrow x=y)$, and $(\forall x,y,z\in P)(((x\leq y)\land(y\leq z))\Rightarrow x\leq z)$.
content.formula: $$\operatorname{Poset}(P,\leq)\iff$$ $$\begin{aligned}&x\leq x &&\text{(Reflexivity)}\\&(x\leq y)\land(y\leq x) \Rightarrow x=y &&\text{(Antisymmetry)}\\&(x\leq y)\land(y\leq z)\Rightarrow x\leq z &&\text{(Transitivity)}\end{aligned}$$
content.intuition: A partial order provides a consistent notion of one object lying below, preceding, being contained in, or carrying no more information than another. Unlike a total order, it does not require every pair of elements to be comparable. Thus a poset describes a branching hierarchy rather than necessarily a single linear arrangement.

examples.content: For any set $X$, the power set $(\mathcal P(X),\subseteq)$ is a poset. Set inclusion is reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive, while two subsets may be incomparable.
The positive integers ordered by divisibility form the poset $(\mathbb N_{>0},\mid)$, where $m\mid n$ means that there exists $k\in\mathbb N_{>0}$ such that $n=mk$.

content.statement: An upper bound for a subset of a partially ordered set is an element lying above every element of that subset.
content.formal: Let $(P,\leq)$ be a partially ordered set and let $A\subseteq P$. An element $b\in P$ is an upper bound for $A$ if $a\leq b$ for every $a\in A$.
content.intuition: An upper bound is a single object that contains, extends, or dominates every object in the family. It does not have to belong to the family itself.

examples.content: If $A=\{A_i:i\in I\}$ is a chain of subsets ordered by inclusion, then $\bigcup_{i\in I}A_i$ is an upper bound for $A$.

edges.notes: A partial order is a relation on a set satisfying reflexivity, antisymmetry, and transitivity.
A poset is a set together with a partial order.
Zorn's lemma is stated for partially ordered sets.
